articles.title: Israel ready for another Iran war, but Trump has yet to decide
articles.body:
Israel's military has completed its preparations for another confrontation with Iran, both defensive and offensive, and the country's readiness is considered exceptionally high. But while Israel is increasingly prepared for renewed fighting, the decision on whether to launch another military campaign rests with Washington, not Jerusalem.
President Donald Trump faces two options. He could continue negotiating with Tehran in an effort to secure an agreement on more favorable terms for the United States, or he could resume military strikes alongside Israel. For now, he is pursuing both tracks, keeping negotiations alive while stepping up military preparations.
What remains unclear is precisely what Trump hopes to achieve through another military campaign and, more importantly, how he intends to bring it to an end. There is still no clear indication of what military objectives would justify renewed strikes, what would constitute success or how the fighting could be brought to a close.
As previously reported, Israel's political and military leadership did not want to initiate a strike before the elections, but preparations continued at an accelerated pace. Those preparations are now complete, following close coordination with the United States. American officials are already familiar with Israel's capabilities after the IDF's performance during Operation Roaring Lion, including its strikes in Iran, where it achieved complete air superiority, and its defensive operations.
The buildup is increasingly visible. Ten U.S. military transport aircraft arrived at Israeli Air Force bases this week as part of an airlift delivering military equipment to the region. Additional American forces are also being deployed. This goes beyond political rhetoric: Equipment, supplies and military capabilities are being positioned for the possibility of renewed fighting.
The Israeli Air Force has also been conducting exercises designed to demonstrate its readiness. According to foreign reports, dozens of Israeli fighter jets and refueling aircraft flew over Syria and Iraq, reaching an area near the Iranian border before returning to Israel.
The reports said Israel notified the Americans in advance that the flights were an exercise intended to demonstrate its capabilities to Tehran. Rather than routine training, the flights rehearsed a possible scenario for another strike. The Air Force reportedly conducted the exercise more than once.
US military options are taking shape, but the objectives remain unclear
According to The Wall Street Journal, U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper presented Trump with military options for renewed strikes against Iran. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine also attended the meeting.
The high-level discussion underscores how seriously Washington is considering military action even as diplomatic contacts continue. According to the report, however, Trump has yet to decide whether to resume the fighting.
His public statements offer another indication of his thinking. Two days ago, Trump wrote: "Everyone knows we had to strike Iran. They are not going to have nuclear weapons, and all of this is going to end very soon."
Combined with the military discussions at the White House and the buildup of forces in the region, the message suggests that Trump is preparing for the possibility of a short campaign. But there is no guarantee Iran would accept his timetable, and it remains unclear how Washington would bring such a confrontation to an end.
Both Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would enter another campaign following elections in their respective countries. Netanyahu would remain in office as caretaker prime minister. Israeli law does not prohibit a caretaker government from deciding to go to war, but such a decision requires approval from the government or an authorized security Cabinet. The prime minister cannot make it alone.
A central concern is the lack of clarity about Washington's objectives. If Trump is considering a short air campaign against Iran's nuclear infrastructure, missile systems and military capabilities, even a highly effective operation would not necessarily topple the Iranian regime.
Regime change is a broader strategic objective that cannot be guaranteed through a series of successful airstrikes. Significant military achievements do not necessarily mean Iran's leadership will fall or change its policies.
Alternatively, Trump may be seeking to use military pressure to extract better terms from Tehran at the negotiating table. If that is the objective, the details of any eventual agreement will matter as much as the pressure used to secure it. From Israel's perspective, a deal that merely postpones another confrontation without addressing Iran's principal threats would leave the underlying problem unresolved.
There is also the possibility of renewed fighting in Lebanon. Hezbollah joined the previous confrontation during Operation Roaring Lion, and another campaign against Iran could again develop into a war on two fronts.
A U.S. plan for a campaign lasting only a few days would not prevent Iran or Hezbollah from seeking to prolong it. Both could attempt to widen the conflict, target Israel and American interests in the region and extend the fighting well beyond Trump's intended timetable.
The IDF must therefore prepare for a potentially longer conflict, including the demands it would place on Israel's air defenses, interceptor stockpiles and the readiness of its forces.
Diplomatic contacts continue as Iran warns it will decide when a war ends
Meanwhile, reports suggest there may be progress in negotiations between Washington and Tehran. The Qatari newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed reported a breakthrough in indirect talks and said an American delegation had joined discussions in Doha in an effort to move toward direct negotiations.
An Iranian source cited in the report said one of Iran's deputy foreign ministers was in Qatar and that the talks were being conducted through a mediator.
According to the report, discussions have focused on initial steps concerning Iran's nuclear program, the Strait of Hormuz and economic incentives for Tehran. China and Russia could also serve as guarantors of a possible agreement.
The reports do not mean a deal is imminent. They do, however, indicate that diplomacy remains active alongside the military preparations. Significant disagreements persist over three main issues: the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's nuclear program and its missiles. Trump has addressed Hormuz and the nuclear issue, while Israel is also seeking to halt Iran's military buildup.
Tehran, meanwhile, is escalating its warnings. Against the backdrop of the reported negotiations, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei published a series of messages following a meeting with senior military officials.
"Any threat, at any level and of any kind, must be met with an immediate, significant response without geographical restrictions," he wrote.
Khamenei also warned that if strikes against Iran resume, the country's armed forces and people will decide "when and under what conditions they will end."
The contrast is clear. Trump says the confrontation will be over very soon. Khamenei insists Iran will determine when the fighting ends and on what terms. Between those competing positions lies the possibility of another war whose duration and scale neither side may be able to control.
Another important factor is Washington's view of Israel as a major operational partner. The IDF's performance during Operation Roaring Lion, in both offensive and defensive operations, and the close coordination between the two militaries have strengthened Israel's standing with the Americans.
The American airlift, military coordination and joint preparations all point to substantial cooperation. But close military cooperation does not mean the two countries necessarily share the same strategic priorities.
Trump will ultimately make decisions based on American interests. Israel must ensure that any renewed military campaign also serves its own long-term security needs.
The decision now rests with Trump. He must determine whether the military buildup is intended to pressure Tehran into accepting a new agreement or whether it is preparation for another joint military campaign.
But before either course is chosen, the central question needs an answer: What is the strategic objective, and what would constitute victory?
Another strike against Iran is not necessarily the problem. The greater risk is entering another war without a clear plan for ending it or a realistic understanding of what comes afterward.

articles.title: Iran's Khamenei orders unrestricted response to threats
articles.body:
This live blog has concluded
Breadcrumb
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has warned the United States and Israel against resuming attacks, ordering the country's armed forces to prepare for any renewed conflict and bring all US and Israeli assets within striking range.
The warnings come amid continuing tensions between Tehran and Washington, with diplomatic efforts to secure an agreement ongoing.
Other updates:
Iran's supreme leader on Saturday warned the United States and Israel against launching new attacks on the country following their threats to resume their strikes after crucial elections, as fears mount over a return to fighting.
The declaration came as the Islamic republic's top diplomat said there were no plans to hold talks with the United States, as indirect mediation via Qatar continues.
President Donald Trump has warned of fresh military action after the United States holds midterm elections early next week, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying on Saturday "we can achieve military objectives if we seek to".
In Israel, which is coming off fresh elections, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has spoken of a "historic, one-time opportunity" to topple the Iranian government.
Polls in both countries could determine the direction of the conflict, with Israel having voted Tuesday but yet to form a new government.
"Any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response," Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei told top military commanders in a meeting, according to a statement.
The encounter was the first reported meeting between Khamenei and military top brass, and included armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, army chief Amir Hatami and Revolutionary Guards commander Ahmad Vahidi.
The supreme leader has not been seen publicly since before he took the helm in March after the killing of his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in US-Israeli strikes.
Khamenei also ordered commanders to update Iran's target list to include "all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist enemy".
Iran has previously warned it would consider severing undersea cables in the Strait of Hormuz.
The United Nations on Saturday condemned the "heartbreaking" death of one of its employees in Yemen under custody of the Houthis and demanded an inquiry.
Mohammad al-Shami, a staff member of the UN Human Rights Office in Yemen, had been "arbitrarily held" by the Houthis since June 2024, the organisation said in a statement.
It cited his family as saying he had died more than a month ago but that his relatives had only been recently informed.
The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Turk, said in the statement that no explanation had been given for the "heartbreaking loss".
The Iran-aligned Houthis are fighting against Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.
The statement said Turk "demanded full transparency from the Houthi authorities and an urgent, independent and thorough investigation into his death".
Iran is debating whether to maintain its longstanding ban on nuclear weapons in the event that hostilities resume, although no decision on any changes has been taken, security chief Mohsen Rezaei told state TV on Saturday.
British police on Saturday arrested at least 139 Palestine Action supporters, who protested in London and Edinburgh days ahead of a court appeal over the government's contentious ban of the group.
London's Metropolitan Police began detaining people shortly after hundreds started a lunchtime "mass action" outside the US Embassy, according to reports.
The force said in an evening update that officers were "continuing to make arrests" as they confirmed that 139 had already been detained.
Police have arrested more than 4,000 people on suspicion of showing support for Palestine Action, according to campaigners, after the British government outlawed it under anti-terror laws in July 2025.
Many of those arrested, including senior citizens and Holocaust survivors, have displayed signs at rallies reading: "I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action."
In July, hearings related to more than 2,000 of those cases were postponed until later this year.
"It is truly dystopian that there have now been over 4,000 arrests under terror laws for peaceful vigils," Protest organisers Defend Our Juries said in a statement.
Regional leaders called for calm Saturday as fears of a new escalation between the US, Israel and Iran grow.
On Saturday, Saudi Arabia's vice minister of foreign affairs said the message from the region is that it wants a return to peace. Speaking at a security forum in Bahrain, Waleed ElKhereiji told the audience that efforts were being made to prevent a military escalation and reach an agreement that ends the crisis with Iran.
“If you look at … the efforts that everybody is trying to do, the message is very clear. People in this part of the world want to bring peace back to the region," he said. But he said no one can predict the outcome of the efforts.
Concerns are rising about a return to an all-out Iran war.
Speaking at the same event, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said an escalation in the region would be extremely destructive.
“We are very confident that … the second round will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere,” he said.
Syria's Foreign Minister said Saturday that border security is a shared responsibility between his country and Jordan and that a high-level meeting is expected next month to discuss arrangements.
Speaking Saturday at the security forum in Bahrain, Assad al-Shibani said there are no “skirmishes” between the countries.
The announcement came after Jordanian strikes in Syria raised tensions between the neighbors.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said Tehran is prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz on its own terms, arguing that an agreement over the strategic waterway could pave the way for renewed negotiations with Washington.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, Araghchi said Iran was demanding international recognition of a new shipping route agreed with Oman, alongside the closure of other routes through the strait.
He said Tehran's conditions also included lifting sanctions imposed after the Islamabad memorandum of understanding and reducing US military forces in the region.
Araghchi described Iran's proposal as the only plan currently on the table to restore shipping through the waterway, which has been heavily disrupted since the US-Israeli war on Iran began.
He added that mediators had presented proposals on the nuclear issue, which Tehran was reviewing.
While describing Washington's efforts to establish broader dialogue with Iran as a positive step, Araghchi said there were currently no plans to meet US officials.
He added that Tehran would decide whether future negotiations would be direct or indirect once Washington accepted its conditions.
Yemen's Foreign Minister Afrah Al-Zuba has condemned the Houthis' siege of Taiz as a war crime, accusing the group of exploiting residents' need for food, medicine and fuel to exert political pressure and blackmail, state news agency Saba reported.
Al-Zuba called for the immediate lifting of the siege and the permanent and safe reopening of roads leading into and out of the city.
Speaking during the third plenary session of the Manama Dialogue 2026 in Bahrain, the minister said ending the Houthis' attempted “coup” and restoring Yemen's state institutions was a collective responsibility shared by members of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC).
She stressed that lasting regional security could not be achieved without a safe and stable Yemen.
“The repercussions of the coup against the state have extended beyond Yemen’s borders, affecting the security of neighbouring countries, navigation, and international interests,” Al-Zuba said in her speech.
“This necessitates translating solidarity into practical steps to address the source of threats and to establish sustainable stability.”
Al-Zuba made history in July 2026 when she became Yemen's first female foreign minister.
Iran said two fishermen it had reported missing on Saturday have now been found, following what it called a US attack on a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.
"Two fishermen from Qeshm, who had gone missing following an attack by the American enemy on their fishing boat this morning, have been found," state television said.
Earlier, state TV had cited a provincial official as saying that two fishermen had gone missing and two others were wounded in what he called an attack by the United States on their vessel in the crucial Hormuz waterway.
Jordanian border guards stopped a group of 14 armed individuals attempting to cross into northern Jordan from Syria, the armed forces said in a statement on Saturday.
The group tried to infiltrate on Friday under heavy fire and direct engagement, causing numerous casualties among the armed group, while the remaining members fled back into Syria, the armed forces said.
Oman said Friday it had rescued 25 sailors from a merchant ship set ablaze in an attack.
Muscat's navy "carried out an evacuation operation for 25 crew members of the merchant ship RITI, flying the Panamanian flag, after it was targeted, which led to a fire breaking out on board," Oman's Maritime Security Centre said in a statement.
The crew members were provided with medical care, the Omani statement said, without giving details.
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has warned the United States against resuming military attacks, saying Tehran will determine the timing and terms of any future conflict if its enemies launch further strikes.
In a statement, Khamenei also ordered Iran's armed forces to update their target list to bring “all US and Israeli assets, tangible and intangible” within striking range.
He said Iran would decide how and when any new conflict would end if its enemies resumed military or terrorist attacks.
He also called on the military to strengthen its intelligence capabilities and develop domestic defence capabilities, while ordering an increase in the production of ammunition and weapons for reconnaissance, support and combat operations.
Khamenei said Iran would decide how and when any new conflict would end if its enemies resumed military or terrorist attacks.
Iran's army warned Saturday that any new US attack would only spread their war wider, following threats by America and Israel of further military action as they hold crucial elections.
The Iranian warning comes with fresh diplomatic efforts underway to avert a resumption of fighting, with Qatari mediators in Tehran and US Vice President JD Vance reportedly sending a letter to Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei.
"If the US president once again embarks on more regional adventurism under pressure from, and in an attempt to appease, the Zionists, the flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area," Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said in a post on X, without elaborating.
Two fishermen were missing and two others injured in an attack on two boats in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, an official said, blaming the United States for the incident.
"An attack by the American enemy occurred around 11:30 (0800 GMT) today on two fishing boats, each carrying two people, near Qeshm Island," said Ahmad Nafisi, deputy provincial governor of Hormozgan province, according to state TV.
"Two of those were transported to Qeshm and the other two remain missing while search and rescue operations are currently underway to locate them," he added.
Turkey has officially nominated a former foreign minister and yearslong ambassador to the United Nations for the next UN secretary-general, state-run media reported Saturday.
The next UN chief will succeed António Guterres, who has led the world body for almost 10 years. The organization is under pressure to reform as it finds itself sidelined in wars in Iran, Ukraine and Gaza while also facing a financial crisis that has forced major cuts to humanitarian and development programs.
Feridun Sinirlioglu, a 70-year-old former Turkish foreign minister and UN diplomat, had floated his candidacy on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly’s high-level meeting in New York last month.
Sinirlioglu was Turkey's top diplomat for a few months in 2015, an interim period between elections, and its UN ambassador between 2016 and 2023. He currently serves as the secretary-general of the Vienna-based Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
His current three-year mandate is scheduled to end in December 2027, but the top UN job would have a Jan. 1 start date.
Ahmet Yildiz, Turkey’s current representative to the UN, told the Anadolu news agency that Sinirlioglu's name was officially submitted with backing from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Erdogan has been vocal in calling for reform of the UN Security Council, especially criticizing the dominance of its five permanent members. Sinirlioglu is likely to reflect the president’s agenda.
The next U.N. secretary-general will be decided by the 15-nation UN Security Council, especially its five veto-wielding members — the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France. The 193-member General Assembly must give final approval.
Syria's top diplomat on Saturday said Damascus was considering whether to join the Mecca alliance that binds Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in a Nato-style defence pact.
"Discussions are currently underway to evaluate Syria's entry into the Mecca alliance," Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said during the IISS Manama Dialogue event in Bahrain.
Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, citing a Hormozgan province official, said on Saturday that the US attacked two fishing boats near Qeshm Island, leaving two fishermen missing and one wounded.
There was no immediate US confirmation of the attack.
Iran has warned of major retaliation if attacked again, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi threatening an “earth-shattering blow” as tensions across the region continue to escalate.
The latest warnings come amid renewed diplomatic efforts to secure a deal between Tehran and Washington, with Qatari mediators returning to Iran and Egypt voicing concern over another escalation.
Meanwhile, drone attacks have been reported off Iran’s Qeshm Island, while Saudi Arabia says it intercepted drones over Riyadh and several other regions.
Follow The New Arab for the latest developments as the Iran war continues to threaten regional stability.

articles.title: U.S. clears sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine
articles.body:
- The U.S. State Department approved a possible $2.1 billion sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptors to Ukraine on Oct. 30.
- Canada, Germany and Norway are funding part of the sale through JUMPSTART, with the rest financed by the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan.
The U.S. State Department has approved a possible sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE interceptors to Ukraine for its Patriot air defense systems, a package worth an estimated $2.1 billion that will be paid for entirely by Ukraine’s allies and partners. The department notified Congress of the decision on Oct. 30.
Canada, Germany and Norway are contributing donations through JUMPSTART, a U.S. Foreign Military Sales mechanism for donor-funded Ukraine purchases, and Ukraine will cover the rest with national funds financed by the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan. No U.S. funds are involved. Besides the missiles, the package includes classified and unclassified PAC-3 MSE spare parts and logistics and program support. Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor.
The notification is not a contract. It opens a congressional review period, after which Ukraine and the U.S. government can sign a letter of offer and acceptance and the U.S. Army can place the order with Lockheed Martin. The State Department gave no delivery schedule, and it did not say how the cost will be split among the three donors and the EU-financed share. Divided evenly, the total comes to about $4.2 million per missile, but that figure also covers spares and support.
The State Department said the missiles will help Ukraine sustain its existing Patriot operations against ongoing aerial threats, and that Ukraine will have no difficulty absorbing them into its armed forces. The sale will not require any additional U.S. government or contractor personnel in Ukraine.
The approval comes days after Ukrainian officials publicly pressed Washington on interceptor supplies. On Oct. 26, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had waited nearly a month for U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to sign off on missiles for its Patriot and NASAMS systems, including transfers from allied stocks that require U.S. approval. A day later, he told journalists that Ukraine had received an average of 12 Patriot interceptors a month from the United States in 2026, while Russia launches about 150 ballistic missiles a month that Ukraine needs to intercept.
PAC-3 MSE is the Patriot system’s main weapon against ballistic missiles. Unlike the older PAC-2 interceptors, which detonate a blast-fragmentation warhead near the target, the PAC-3 family destroys targets by direct impact, a method known as hit-to-kill. The Missile Segment Enhancement version adds a larger two-pulse solid rocket motor, with the second pulse firing late in the flight to extend range and altitude against maneuvering threats. That makes it the interceptor Ukraine relies on against Russian Iskander ballistic missiles and Kh-47M2 Kinzhal air-launched missiles. Ukrainian officials have described PAC-3 as their only effective defense against Russian ballistic missiles.
Ukraine received its first Patriot battery in April 2023, and in May of that year Ukrainian crews shot down a Kinzhal over Kyiv, the first publicly confirmed combat interception of the missile. Ukraine has since received further batteries from the United States, Germany, the Netherlands and Romania, and in July 2025 Germany and Norway agreed to pay for three more systems to be bought from the U.S. manufacturer. Interceptor supply has been a tighter constraint than launchers. In February 2026, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius offered five PAC-3 rounds from German stocks if other allies together supplied 30 more, and in July, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said it was using about $1 billion from the EU loan to buy roughly 100 Patriot missiles.
The financing reflects how Ukraine’s air defense is now paid for. The U.S. Defense Security Cooperation Agency describes JUMPSTART as a channel that lets allies and partners finance Ukraine’s Foreign Military Sales cases with their own donations. Norway reported routing about NOK 10 billion through the mechanism in 2025, much of it for F-16 support. In September 2026, Canada said it would put about C$350 million toward air defense interceptors for Ukraine through JUMPSTART. Separately, NATO allies buy U.S. weapons for Ukraine through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, known as PURL.
EU governments agreed in early 2026 on a €90 billion loan for 2026 and 2027, with €60 billion set aside for defense, and the first disbursements went out in June 2026. The loan gives priority to weapons built in Ukraine, the EU and the European Economic Area, but allows purchases elsewhere when no European alternative exists. Patriot interceptors are one case where none does.
Production is the main limit on how fast the missiles can arrive. Lockheed Martin delivered 620 PAC-3 MSE interceptors in 2025, a company record. In January 2026, the company and the U.S. Department of War signed a seven-year framework agreement to raise annual output from about 600 to roughly 2,000. In April, the U.S. Army awarded Lockheed a $4.76 billion PAC-3 MSE contract, most of it funded through Foreign Military Sales customers. Demand has also climbed since the United States drew on its own Patriot inventory during this year’s conflict with Iran.
At 2025 production rates, the 500 missiles approved for Ukraine equal about 10 months of Lockheed’s output. Where Ukraine’s order falls in the production queue, and when the first missiles from this sale will reach Patriot batteries in Ukraine, has not been disclosed.

articles.title: First the radars, then the rest: Iran's methodical assault on US bases
articles.body:
Iran's campaign against American military bases across the Middle East began with a calculated assault on the systems designed to detect incoming missiles and drones, before expanding to aircraft, hangars, warehouses and troop facilities, according to an Associated Press investigation that reveals extensive damage to the U.S. military's regional infrastructure.
An analysis of satellite imagery, corroborated by interviews with four regional officials familiar with the damage, found that more than 115 drone and missile strikes claimed by Iran or Iranian-backed militias had damaged or destroyed structures at 26 military bases and other sites housing American equipment through August. The strikes caused billions of dollars in equipment damage and forced significant changes to the U.S. military's deployment across the region.
Two regional officials told the AP that Washington has moved substantial military assets out of the Persian Gulf, including aircraft, air defense systems, communications equipment and other essential infrastructure. The findings raise questions about the vulnerability of America's regional bases as President Donald Trump considers renewed military action against Iran after the November 3 midterm elections, with Tehran threatening a major response.
The investigation offers a more detailed picture of the damage than the U.S. government has publicly disclosed during the eight-month conflict. From April through June alone, hundreds of buildings and other structures were damaged or destroyed. U.S. Central Command, which oversees American military operations in the Middle East, has repeatedly declined to provide detailed assessments, citing operational security, and did not comment on the AP's findings. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell maintained that American forces remained adequately protected and fully equipped to continue operations against Iran.
Iran's first targets: the eyes of US air defenses
The sequence of attacks reveals a deliberate pattern. Rather than immediately concentrating on barracks and other buildings, Iranian forces initially targeted the radar systems responsible for detecting and tracking incoming threats. Within the first two days of the war in late February, strikes destroyed protective enclosures around American radar installations at Camp Arifjan in Kuwait and Naval Support Activity Bahrain. Portable radars at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan were also hit.
Among the most consequential losses was a radar in Jordan reported to have been destroyed. According to manufacturer Raytheon, the U.S. Army possesses only 13 of these specialized systems worldwide, with budget documents indicating that each costs approximately $500 million. Another radar in Qatar sustained extensive damage, although investigators could not determine whether it had been destroyed. The system had been purchased as part of a $1.1 billion agreement in 2013 and appeared to be the only one of its kind in the region.
N.R. Jenzen-Jones, director of the technical intelligence consultancy Armament Research Services, said the attacks appeared designed to weaken the ability of American and allied forces to respond to subsequent strikes. By targeting expensive, difficult-to-replace early-warning equipment, Iran was striking at a critical component of the regional air defense network.
Once the initial radar attacks had been carried out, Iranian forces broadened their targets. During the first month of fighting, more than 50 successful strikes hit 18 locations containing American military equipment, with particular attention paid to areas housing aircraft. The targets eventually expanded to include fuel storage facilities, communications infrastructure, warehouses and troop accommodations.
Kuwait's bases take the heaviest damage
Kuwait suffered the greatest concentration of Iranian attacks, although American installations in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates were also hit. At Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait, at least 30 strikes damaged or destroyed 15 aircraft hangars, numerous warehouses and 10 buildings near a residential area.
Camp Buehring, another major American installation in Kuwait, sustained particularly widespread destruction. Most of its aircraft hangars were rendered inoperable, while facilities used by troops suffered extensive damage. The base's gym was destroyed in March, a store serving personnel was hit in late July, and strikes also severely damaged a garage and dining facility, according to regional officials familiar with the attacks.
The scale of destruction became clearer only months later, when high-resolution satellite images became available. Between early March and late August, more than 30 structures at Camp Buehring were damaged or destroyed. The AP identified multiple strikes on the installation during March, April, May and July.
Kuwait was also the site of the deadliest known Iranian attack on American troops during the war. On March 1, six U.S. service members were killed when a drone struck Port Shuaiba, underscoring that the attacks threatened personnel as well as expensive military equipment.
Other countries sustained significant losses. At Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, an Iranian strike damaged the rear section of a Boeing E-3 Sentry airborne surveillance aircraft. A regional military official who visited the installation described extensive destruction, including damaged barracks, dining halls and scattered debris. The official said several other aircraft had also been hit, including two aerial refueling tankers. Another Iranian strike damaged a CIA unit at the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh.
At Al Dhafra Air Base, approximately 20 miles (32 kilometers) south of Abu Dhabi, repeated attacks early in the conflict damaged aircraft hangars, other infrastructure and equipment, including an early-warning radar and surveillance drones. A Congressional Research Service report updated in October identified 15 American aircraft damaged at regional bases.
Satellite restrictions concealed the extent of damage
Assessing the destruction has been complicated by restrictions on commercial satellite imagery. Major providers holding U.S. government contracts blocked or delayed the public release of images following requests from American officials, sometimes citing national security concerns. This limited independent scrutiny of damaged installations, with some high-resolution images becoming available only months after the attacks.
To complete its investigation, the AP obtained imagery from OneAtlas, a satellite service owned by Airbus, and compared it with other available evidence. The resulting assessment provides a broader picture of the damage than previous official disclosures, including reports from the Pentagon's inspector general, although the military has not released a comprehensive public accounting of the losses.
The findings also highlight a broader problem confronting modern militaries: the growing vulnerability of large, fixed installations to sustained attacks involving relatively inexpensive drones and missiles. Raphael Cohen, director of the National Security Program at the RAND School of Public Policy, said even heavily equipped military forces are increasingly exposed to such threats.
"This should be a wake-up call for the United States," Cohen said.
With Washington and Tehran both leaving open the possibility of renewed fighting, further damage could deepen the uncertainty surrounding America's long-term military presence in the Persian Gulf. It remains unclear whether the United States will rebuild its damaged bases and equipment once the war ends or fundamentally rethink how its forces are positioned and protected.
For Cohen, the destruction points to a lasting shift in military strategy. The era in which American forces could depend on large, permanent bases as relatively secure platforms for operations, he argued, may be coming to an end.

articles.title: Iran lawmakers call for withdrawal from NPT: Will we have war or peace?
articles.body:
Iran lawmakers call for withdrawal from NPT: Will we have war or peace?
Withdrawal from the nuclear treaty doses not mean that Iran would build a nuclear weapon, observers say.
Several Iranian lawmakers have called for the country’s withdrawal from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), as United States President Donald Trump says the war on Iran will be “wrapped up” soon.
The lawmakers’ demands come as Qatari mediators returned to Tehran this week to mediate peace talks with the US.
Before the US and Israel’s war on Iran began on February 28, Washington and Tehran had already been engaging in indirect nuclear negotiations mediated by Oman. Iran had also stated on numerous occasions that it had no plans to develop nuclear weapons.
Trump has also repeatedly stated that Iran “cannot have a nuclear weapon”, making it a non-negotiable condition for ending the ongoing conflict and securing a permanent deal.
Iran, however, has demanded certain conditions be met before it will talk again about its nuclear programme – including an end to the US naval blockade of its ports in and around the Strait of Hormuz, the lifting of sanctions and a guarantee there will be no more attacks.
The war, which is entering its ninth month, has upended global energy and financial markets with the closure of Hormuz.
On Friday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi hit back at Friedrich Merz after the German chancellor said the war on Iran has added more than 100 billion euros ($112bn) to Europe’s energy costs.
In a post on X, Araghchi noted that Merz had “hailed” the US and Israel’s attacks on Iran in June of last year, when he said: “This is the dirty work Israel is doing for all of us.”
The Iranian foreign minister then warned that any renewed attacks could come at a far higher cost for Europe.
“100bn Euro is nothing compared to the Earth-shattering blow Iran’s Powerful Armed Forces will deal against those who dare harm our people,” Araghchi wrote. “Red lines are a thing of the past,” he added.
Could Iran withdraw from the NPT, and what would that mean for diplomatic efforts to end the war?
Here’s what we know:
Which Iranian lawmakers are calling for withdrawal from the NPT, and why?
On Saturday, Iranian legislator Mahmoud Nabavian called for Iran to withdraw from the NPT and change its nuclear doctrine, adding to similar demands from other lawmakers and public figures.
“Now that we have paid the heavy costs of war and sanctions, it is time for the Iranian nation to withdraw from the NPT treaty and change the nuclear doctrine,” he wrote on X.
In parliament, Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of the National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, said 10 proposals to withdraw from the treaty had been registered, and withdrawal was under consideration, according to the Fars news agency.
Mohammad Javad Haj Ali Akbari, an Iranian politician and scholar, also called for a review of Iran’s nuclear doctrine, describing it as a “national demand” during his sermon on Friday, state broadcaster IRIB reported.
He said the demand was not a hasty or emotional reaction, but reflected Iranians’ awareness of what he described as US failures to honour commitments.
Separately, in a report earlier this week, Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported calls for Iran to withdraw from the NPT and accused the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) of becoming politically aligned with the US and Israel.
Last month, an IAEA resolution expressed “grave concerns” about Iran’s “continued noncompliance” with its obligations under the NPT, to which it is a signatory.
But the IAEA has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since the US and Israel launched a 12-day war against the country in June 2025, which included attacks on key Iranian nuclear sites, such as the Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan facilities.
Iran has condemned the IAEA resolution, calling it baseless and politically motivated.
What is the NPT?
The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons is a landmark international treaty aimed at preventing the spread of nuclear weapons and promoting peaceful uses of nuclear energy.
It was opened for signature on July 1, 1968, and entered into force on March 5, 1970. The treaty was negotiated by the US, the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom.
Under the NPT, nuclear-weapon states agree not to transfer nuclear weapons or assist non-nuclear-weapon states in developing them.
Non-nuclear-weapon states also agree not to seek or acquire nuclear weapons.
The treaty views nuclear-weapon states as those which manufactured and tested a nuclear weapon or other nuclear device before January 1, 1967. Those countries are the US, UK, France, China and Russia. The treaty also paves a path for these original nuclear weapons powers to phase out their arsenals.
A total of 191 countries are now part of the treaty. Non-signatories include India, Pakistan, Israel and South Sudan.
The treaty supports the right of all signatories to access nuclear technology for peaceful purposes under safeguards overseen by the United Nations nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).
Among the 11 articles of the treaty, one allows a country to withdraw with three months’ notice “if it decides that extraordinary events … have jeopardised the supreme interests of its country”.
Iran signed the NPT in July 1968 and ratified it in February 1970 as a nonnuclear-weapon state.
It has since stated consistently that its nuclear programme is for peaceful purposes and research only. The IAEA has conducted inspections under the treaty’s safeguards system.
Has there been any response from Iran’s leaders?
Iranian leaders have not yet responded to demands from lawmakers to withdraw from the NPT.
But on October 24, according to Iranian media reports, the Paydari Front, a hardline faction aligned with conservative groups, also called on parliament to withdraw from the NPT.
Withdrawal from the NPT would not automatically mean that Iran would build a nuclear weapon. Officially, the Iranian government’s position on not seeking nuclear arms remains unchanged.
In June, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs noted that lawmakers are preparing a bill to withdraw Tehran from the NPT.
“In light of recent developments, we will take an appropriate decision,” ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei had said at a news conference. “[The] government has to enforce parliament bills, but such a proposal is just being prepared, and we will coordinate in the later stages with parliament.”
But Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian has said Tehran’s policies align with Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei’s longstanding religious edict against weapons of mass destruction. “The Zionist regime is the only possessor of weapons of mass destruction in the region,” Baghaei had said, referring to the Israeli government.
What has Trump said about ‘wrapping up’ the war?
The US President has repeatedly stated that Iran “cannot have a nuclear weapon” and made this a non-negotiable condition for ending the ongoing conflict and securing a permanent deal.
In a speech at Daytona Beach, Florida late on Friday, he brought up Iran several times and repeated claims about destroying its navy and air force. “We are never going to give them a nuclear weapon,” he said.
Trump also denied that the US had started the war, saying, “This was a war they started many years ago,” and “Iran has been waging war on America since 1979.″
Separately, in an interview with Kansas City radio station KCMO on Friday, he said the war is “going to get wrapped up soon” but said Washington needs “a guarantee there’ll never be a nuclear weapon”.
Mohamed Elmenshawy, a Washington-based analyst, told Al Jazeera that Trump wants to end the standoff with Iran “whether through peace or war as quickly as possible”, and may launch new attacks after the November 3 midterm elections.
“What breaks this state of stalemate, this condition of ‘no peace, no war’, is either achieving some progress in the negotiating track, or the attacks beginning anew,” Elmenshawy told Al Jazeera.
He said Trump believes “time is on his side”, pointing to “strict economic pressure” on Iran, including the US naval blockade that has curtailed Tehran’s ability to export oil as well as sanctions on Iranian aviation and land border closures by several other countries.
Elmenshawy said Tehran “must realise” Trump will not let the conflict “remain suspended like this” and that this pressure should push “the Qatari and Pakistani mediators to drive the efforts more forcefully in order to avoid the path of war”.
Trump faces “pressure from the Israeli side to launch the attacks, and opposite pressure from the Arab Gulf side to push the negotiating track”, he added, saying Trump, “whose next moves cannot be predicted”, could yield to either.
On Saturday, the spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Mohammad Akraminia, sent a warning to US President Donald Trump, writing on X that its armed forces are “closely monitoring America’s movements in the region”.
Akraminia said that if the US president “resorts to another adventure in the region” along with Israel, then Iran will retaliate significantly.
“There is no doubt that the flames of war will engulf a much wider area, and the end of the conflict will not be in his [Trump’s] hands,” Akraminia wrote.
“Given the US President’s track record of betraying diplomacy,” and citing Trump’s “distrustful” nature, Akraminia said the IRGC’s armed forces are “relentlessly enhancing their combat readiness”.
What was the position before the war began?
Before the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28 this year, Tehran and Washington were in active nuclear negotiations.
At talks in Geneva, mediator Oman said both countries had made “significant progress”.
Just one day before the US-Israeli attacks started, Oman’s foreign minister said Iran had agreed to reduce its nuclear stockpiles to “the lowest level possible”. Then the war began.
Almost eight months later, the war has brought this position no further forward.
In fact, more problems, with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz upending global energy markets and most recently, the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi Arabia locking horns, have threatened the Middle East’s regional stability.
Furthermore, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera in September that Iran no longer trusts negotiations with Washington because attacks had come during previous rounds of talks.
Christopher Featherstone, associate lecturer at the Department of Politics and International Relations at the University of York in the UK, told Al Jazeera that the war has set the potential for negotiations all the way back to square one, and it will take significant diplomatic effort to initiate any meaningful negotiations, let alone achieve success in those negotiations.
“Intermediaries will be cautious about being seen to be too close to the US if the conflict reignites, and Iran has shown a strong willingness to reject a ‘deal’ that would favour the Trump administration too heavily,” he said.
What diplomatic efforts are happening to de-escalate the war?
On Friday morning, Qatari mediators, in coordination with US officials, returned to Tehran in an apparent bid to revive the June ceasefire that quickly fell apart over control of the Strait of Hormuz.
Days earlier, they delivered a letter from US Vice President JD Vance to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, proposing renewed peace talks, according to US media.
Iranian sources have confirmed to Al Jazeera that Tehran received a letter from the US on ending the war and suggested the Qatari delegation had come to collect Iran’s response.
The sources said a meeting to discuss a new diplomatic path could be held within a week, either in Doha or Istanbul.
Meanwhile, Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, spokesman for Pakistan’s military, told the Reuters news agency his country is “cautiously optimistic” about mediation efforts between Iran and the US as regional countries seek to revive a ceasefire in the eight-month-old war.
He suggested on Friday that there were positive signs in attempts to de-escalate the conflict. His comments to Reuters were the first since a high-level delegation visited Tehran this week.
Ali al-Sari, a former member of Iran’s parliament, said there are positive indications from both Tehran and Washington on the diplomatic track, despite a military buildup on both sides.
“The response has not been clear so far, but there are indications on the Iranian side, and also in my view on the American side, that the signs are somewhat positive rather than negative,” al-Sari told Al Jazeera.
He said the US is reinforcing its military buildup, while Iran is strengthening its forces “in the Strait of Hormuz and along the borders”. He added that “the coincidence of this message with the Qatari mediation is significant.
“For this reason, Tehran is studying its response carefully and has not rushed, but it wants something in return, even amid a tense situation between the two parties,” he said.
He pointed to the repeated visits of the Qatari delegation, which “came, then returned, then came again”. In his view, this suggests that the Qatari mediation and other mediation efforts, including Russia’s mediation, mean coordination with the US is continuing and is a “positive sign”. Al-Sari also highlighted the US ambassador to Turkiye Tom Barrack’s recent comments that the US and Iran are “very close” to a deal to de-escalate tensions.
Is peace or renewal of war more likely after the US midterm elections?
Currently, Washington and Tehran have sent mixed signals about whether the eight-month war is heading back to full-scale attacks or towards a peace deal.
On Thursday, the head of US Central Command (CENTCOM), Admiral Brad Cooper, briefed US President Donald Trump on options for renewed attacks on Iran, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported.
The Wall Street Journal also reported that Trump was briefed on options for renewed attacks on Thursday. On the same day, US Senator Chris Murphy said he had been briefed on the war plan and described it as “insane”.
Separately, US media reported that Washington has warned Gulf allies to prepare for potential military action after the November 3 midterm elections.
“There has been little signal from either side of a move to a formal peace, but there is the potential for another cautious temporary ceasefire,” Featherstone said.
“After the midterm elections, if Trump loses both Houses, he will be severely limited in his ability to pursue his domestic agenda. This could push him to be more active on the international stage, and the Iran conflict would likely be a focus for his attention,” he added.
“However, he has set out almost no sign of how he would measure victory or success in this war, so a path out of the conflict is incredibly unclear,” he said.
Abas Aslani, a researcher at the Center for Middle East Strategic Studies in Tehran, said a deep lack of trust lies behind Iran’s failure to respond to the US proposals it has received.
“Washington wants Iran to make concessions on the nuclear issue in advance, but Iran insists on the seven conditions,” Aslani told Al Jazeera, referring to Tehran’s seven-point plan to end the war.
“In Iran, they fear that if they commit and fulfil their obligations, the United States will not honour its obligations and will backtrack. Instead, the United States would launch another attack.”
He noted that Trump is “trying to use this potential agreement to promote it to the public and to use it for electoral purposes in the United States”, while “Iran wants an agreement that will be vital and bring peace to the region.”
Aslani said “the conditions and the sequencing” also remain in dispute.
Iran is using mediators to send a message “that its position has not changed”, he said, but Washington “also insists on its position”.
“We don’t see any tangible progress – but despite this, efforts are still ongoing,” he added.

articles.title: Zelensky: Russia fired 17 ballistic missiles overnight, took no steps toward de-escalation in energy sector
articles.body:
Zelensky: Russia fired 17 ballistic missiles overnight, took no steps toward de-escalation in energy sector
According to Ukrinform, the head of state stated this in his nightly video address.
"Every day, unfortunately, they hit our energy infrastructure, causing extensive damage. Russia's operation against our power generation, our energy grids, and our energy interconnections continues. We are shooting down a significant number of Russian Shaheds, but, unfortunately, not all of them. And ballistic missiles are more difficult to deal with. Seventeen ballistic missiles were launched overnight. A tough challenge, especially when Patriot missiles are in such short supply," Zelensky said.
He noted that throughout the day, energy workers and specialists from the State Emergency Service of Ukraine had been working in Dnipro, Kyiv and the Kyiv region, as well as in other cities and communities, dealing with the aftermath of the attacks and restoring electricity supplies.
"Unfortunately, Dnipro came under repeated strikes throughout the day, including again this evening. The energy infrastructure was hit, and the railway station was hit again as well. Unfortunately, additional emergency power outages have been introduced. We have the personnel and equipment needed for restoration. In Kyiv and the region, in the Chernihiv region, Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv and Sumy regions – restoration work must proceed promptly everywhere. Today, Russian ballistic missiles also struck the Poltava region. Kremenchuk. Our oil refining infrastructure was targeted. The Russians have not taken a single step toward energy de-escalation. They continue to carry out terrorist strikes against our cities," Zelensky said.
At the same time, he stressed that Ukraine would continue working with all its partners to strengthen air defense and secure ammunition for F-16 fighter jets.
"We are preparing new decisions in the near future," the head of state said.
As reported, Russian attacks caused extensive damage to energy infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region and the Dnipropetrovsk region. It will take time to fully restore electricity supplies, the Ukrainian Energy Ministry said.
Emergency power cuts are being implemented in the Dnipropetrovsk region following the Russian attack.

articles.title: US, South Korea, Japan call for ‘complete denuclearisation’ of North Korea
articles.body:
US, South Korea, Japan call for ‘complete denuclearisation’ of North Korea
The joint statement comes as US President Donald Trump seeks a new meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
The United States, South Korea and Japan have reiterated their longstanding call for North Korea to give up its nuclear weapons, a move Pyongyang has repeatedly ruled out.
The three countries addressed the issue on the sidelines of the Group of 20 (G20) meeting in the US city of Atlanta on Thursday, with their top diplomats reaffirming their “resolute commitment to the complete denuclearisation” of North Korea, according to a readout by the US Department of State.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun and Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi also pledged the “full implementation” of United Nations Security Council resolutions, including a ban on supporting revenue for North Korea’s nuclear and ballistic missile programmes.
The statement comes despite repeated overtures to North Korea by US President Donald Trump, who held a series of historic summits with its leader, Kim Jong Un, during his first term in office and has continued to call Kim a “friend”.
Last year, Trump bucked a long-held US policy by conceding that North Korea was already “sort of a nuclear power”.
More recently, he has played down concerns about North Korea’s nuclear programme and expressed a desire to meet Kim again. Speculation is mounting that the two leaders could reconnect at next month’s APEC summit in China, which Trump is due to attend.
Analysts and South Korea’s spy agency say Kim may have conveyed Pyongyang’s position on potential talks with Trump to Beijing during a recent visit to the Chinese border city of Dandong.
South Korea’s dovish President Lee Jae Myung – who has repeatedly offered Pyongyang talks without preconditions – suggested in September that Washington seek a freeze, rather than the immediate elimination, of the North’s nuclear programme in return for sanctions relief.
Critics have said such an approach risks tacitly accepting North Korea as a nuclear-armed state while allowing Pyongyang to win sanctions relief without giving up its arsenal.
Despite long-running UN sanctions, North Korea, which is backed by Russia and China, has enshrined its status as a nuclear-armed state in law. Pyongyang’s government has declared its atomic arsenal to be permanent and irreversible.
Pyongyang denounced a joint statement on Saturday by a group of nations monitoring sanctions implementation against it, pledging that “the stereotyped sanctions racket of the US and the West can neither influence the position of the DPRK (North Korea) as a nuclear weapons state.”

articles.title: US greenlights $2.1bn Patriot missile sale to Ukraine
articles.body:
US greenlights $2.1bn Patriot missile sale to Ukraine
Deal would be one of the most significant steps to supply defensive weapons to Kyiv since Trump took office in 2025.
The United States says it has approved the possible sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1bn.
The package of missiles, parts and support, announced on Friday by the US State Department, would be one of the most significant steps to supply defensive weapons to Kyiv since the start of the second administration of President Donald Trump in January 2025.
The Patriot system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.
Delayed missile deliveries, however, have stoked US-Ukraine tensions after Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for his unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.
Ukraine has long said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves of missiles Russia’s military fires at the country.
Zelenskyy said on Monday that Kyiv had been waiting for almost a month for Washington to sign off on critical missile supplies, as Russia stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian energy and civilian infrastructure.
A Russian drone strike on Thursday killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro.
Five people were killed in daytime strikes on two other cities, and a late-evening missile strike killed one person in the capital, Kyiv, officials said.
Delivery years away
Despite Ukraine’s need for quick deliveries of the missiles, Kyiv is unlikely to receive the Patriot interceptors soon. Weapons sales typically take years to fulfil.
Two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles, which have yet to be made, are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.
Ukraine will pay for the missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway through a programme called US JUMPSTART, along with national funds financed by the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan, the State Department said in its statement.
US weapons manufacturer Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors.
The US Army awarded Lockheed a contract worth up to $58.6bn to produce Patriot interceptor missiles in July.
Lockheed has said the deal would allow it to follow through on a promise to triple PAC-3 production capacity by the end of 2030. It has previously announced that Patriot PAC-3 missile interceptor production would reach 2,000 units annually.
Pentagon negotiators are pressing weapons contractors to speed up production.
The US military’s supply of large quantities of weapons to allies and its own heavy munitions use for its operations in Iran have raised concerns about its inventories of key air defence and precision-guided weapons.

articles.title: Patriot sale to Ukraine approved, but first missiles may be years away
articles.body:
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said deliveries of 500 U.S.-approved PAC-3 MSE interceptors may begin only in several years, too late for this winter.
- He asked the United States for 100 Patriot interceptors a month from existing stocks, replenished later by the newly approved production.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says the 500 Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptors the United States cleared for sale to Ukraine on Oct. 30 will not help this winter, because deliveries may not begin for several years. He asked Washington to send interceptors from existing U.S. and allied stocks now and replace them later from the new production run.
The U.S. State Department notified Congress of the possible $2.1 billion sale on Oct. 30. It is funded by donations from Canada, Germany and Norway through the JUMPSTART mechanism and by Ukrainian national funds drawn from the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan, with no U.S. money involved. The notification gave no delivery schedule.
“Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defense package. However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
Alex Raufoglu, a correspondent for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, reported that the 500 are new-build missiles and that, according to his sources, deliveries are not expected until after 2030. Neither the State Department nor Lockheed Martin has published a delivery date.
Lockheed Martin built 620 PAC-3 MSE interceptors in 2025, and in January it signed a seven-year framework agreement with the U.S. Department of War to raise annual output from about 600 to roughly 2,000. New Foreign Military Sales orders join a queue that already includes U.S. Army replenishment and earlier buys by Poland, Germany, Japan, Gulf states and other operators. A new case also has to clear congressional review, be turned into a signed letter of offer and acceptance, and be placed on contract before the missiles enter that queue.
Zelenskyy asked instead for a winter package of 100 interceptors a month from existing stocks, which would deliver the equivalent of the 500 approved missiles in about five months, with partners’ arsenals replenished later by the production Ukraine and its allies have already paid for.
“The United States, our European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses. Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS, through this production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and our partners would be the right approach,” Zelenskyy wrote.
On Oct. 27, Zelenskyy told journalists that Ukraine had received an average of 12 Patriot interceptors a month from the United States in 2026, a fraction of the 100 a month he is now requesting, while Russia fires roughly 150 ballistic missiles a month that need intercepting. In his post, he said Russia had made more than 30 strikes on critical parts of Ukraine’s power grid in the past two weeks of October alone, targeting electricity, heating and water supplies before winter began.
PAC-3 MSE is the Patriot interceptor Ukraine relies on against ballistic missiles: it destroys its target by direct impact, and its two-pulse motor extends range and altitude against maneuvering threats such as Russia’s Iskander and Kinzhal. Ukraine also uses older PAC-2 interceptors, but Ukrainian officials have repeatedly described PAC-3 as their only effective defense against Russian ballistic missiles. Shortages have pushed Ukrainian crews to engage some ballistic targets with a single interceptor instead of the usual two or more.
In April, Zelenskyy said U.S. deliveries under NATO’s PURL program had not stopped but that Ukraine’s interceptor shortage remained critical. In August, CNN was given access to a Ukrainian Patriot battery that had not fired in six weeks because its launchers had no interceptors to load. On Oct. 19, Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent that U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had not approved the transfer of a significant batch of Patriot interceptors that Ukraine’s allies had already paid for, and suggested the delay was meant to pressure Kyiv. A U.S. government official called those claims “not true.” The Washington Post reported the same day that the Trump administration had not approved transfers of interceptors from partner countries.
Asked about the delayed transfers, Hegseth said on Oct. 20 that Washington’s posture toward Ukraine had not changed, but that the U.S. military wanted to keep as many interceptors as possible for its own forces. U.S. inventories have been drawn down by the war with Iran that began in February; the Center for Strategic and International Studies has estimated that U.S. stocks of Patriot and other interceptors fell by about half during that conflict. The Hill reported this week that President Donald Trump is weighing new military strikes on Iran after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. U.S. officials have not publicly linked that decision to the interceptor transfers.
Citing NATO sources, Euronews reported that allies were pessimistic about Ukraine receiving more interceptors before the midterms, and that NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte had asked Greece and Spain to hand over some of their own interceptors without success.
In September, the European Commission approved €6.1 billion in defense procurement for Ukraine, including PAC-3 interceptors bought under a special exception to the EU loan’s preference for European-made weapons, though it did not disclose how much went to Patriot missiles.
“We are asking for decisions that can guarantee the protection of lives not the day after tomorrow or sometime later, but at the very moment the threat is there – when Russia is killing and destroying,” Zelenskyy wrote.
Zelenskyy thanked President Donald Trump, the State Department and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, with whom he said he had recently discussed PAC-3 interceptors. Washington has not responded publicly to his request for interim deliveries, and the delivery schedule for the 500 missiles approved on Oct. 30 remains undisclosed.

articles.title: Explosions in Hormuz as Trump says Iran ‘wants to talk’
articles.body:
A series of maritime incidents and reported explosions in the Persian Gulf heightened tensions between Iran and the United States on Friday, even as President Donald Trump said Tehran was seeking negotiations and Washington was in no hurry to reach an agreement. 
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed that four oil tankers had struck naval mines and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after ignoring Iranian navigation warnings, while British maritime authorities reported separate incidents involving vessels struck by unidentified projectiles.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO) said a vessel was hit on its port side by an unidentified projectile approximately 40 nautical miles (74 kilometers) south of Iran's Lavan Island in the Persian Gulf. The impact sparked a fire on board, but the crew was reported safe and no environmental damage had been reported. The vessel's identity and the party responsible for the incident remained unknown.
In a separate report, UKMTO said an oil tanker had been struck by an unidentified projectile while leaving the Strait of Hormuz. The agency did not identify those responsible for the attack.
Iran claims four tankers hit mines after ignoring warnings
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said four oil tankers had caught fire following explosions in the strategically vital waterway. According to the IRGC Navy, the fourth tanker was carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil when it struck a naval mine, triggering a powerful explosion and fire.
Iranian officials claimed the tankers had attempted to cross the strait using routes not authorized by Tehran and that at least some had ignored repeated warnings from Iranian forces. Iranian state media also reported that some vessels had switched off their navigation and tracking systems before entering dangerous areas. The claims could not be independently verified.
It remained unclear whether the vessels mentioned in the British maritime warnings were among the four tankers cited by Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
Meanwhile, Omani authorities said they had evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged tanker that was attacked and caught fire near the coast of Musandam governorate, close to the Strait of Hormuz. Authorities did not immediately establish whether the vessel was among those mentioned by Iran.
The latest incidents underscore the continuing threat to commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints. Under normal circumstances, roughly one-fifth of global oil supplies pass through the narrow waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman.
Since the war began in late February, Iran has intensified its efforts to control shipping through the strait, repeatedly warning that vessels attempting to cross without its authorization risk being attacked.
Trump: ‘They want to talk, we have time’
Against the backdrop of escalating maritime tensions, Trump said Friday that diplomatic contacts with Tehran were continuing and emphasized that Washington was under no immediate pressure to reach an agreement.
"There are talks. They want to talk. They keep talking," Trump told reporters at the White House. "We have time, frankly."
Trump described the conflict with Iran as "not a typical war" and claimed it was not imposing significant costs on American taxpayers. He also repeated his assertion that U.S. military operations had eliminated Iran's nuclear threat.
"I spent a lot of money in order to get rid of a nuclear weapon, which we've done," he said.
Earlier Friday, in an interview with Kansas City radio station KCMO, Trump expressed optimism that the confrontation would soon end. "It will end soon," he said, without explaining how an agreement might be reached.
The president reiterated that Washington's central demand for ending the conflict remained a guarantee that Iran would never possess nuclear weapons.
His remarks came just days before the U.S. midterm elections, scheduled for Tuesday, November 3. Trump has previously indicated that he would not order additional strikes against Iran before the elections, but has stopped short of ruling out renewed military action afterward.
According to a report published by the Associated Press this week, U.S. officials warned several Middle Eastern countries and regional allies to prepare for the possibility of renewed strikes against Iran following the elections.
The warnings also addressed the prospect of Iranian retaliation, potentially targeting energy facilities and other critical infrastructure across the region. Two diplomats briefed on the discussions stressed, however, that Trump had not made a final decision on whether to resume military operations.
Qatar pushes for a deal as fears of renewed US strikes grow
As tensions mounted in the Gulf, diplomatic efforts to avert another round of fighting continued Friday with the arrival of a Qatari delegation in Tehran.
According to Iran's official IRNA news agency, the delegation was headed by a senior adviser to Qatar's prime minister and was expected to meet senior Iranian officials to discuss bilateral relations and regional developments.
A source familiar with the negotiations told Reuters that Qatar's mediation efforts were being coordinated with the Trump administration.
Qatar had presented Iran with a draft agreement on Sunday aimed at ending the war, but a senior Iranian official dismissed the proposals as unacceptable and said Tehran would not change its position on the nuclear issue.
The main obstacle remains the sequence of steps toward a possible agreement. Washington insists that Iran's nuclear program be addressed from the beginning of negotiations, while Tehran is demanding that the United States first lift its blockade of Iranian ports and remove sanctions restricting Iranian oil exports.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday that Tehran remained in close contact with mediators and was reviewing proposals that could help advance an Iranian seven-day plan for ending the conflict. He stressed that Iran was still giving diplomacy a chance, despite the substantial differences separating the two sides.
The mediation efforts have also been accompanied by a more direct American approach. According to reports, U.S. Vice President JD Vance sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, as Washington explored possible diplomatic channels.
Iranian authorities confirmed receiving the letter but said they had not yet responded. U.S. media reports indicated that the correspondence concerned the possibility of renewing negotiations, potentially establishing a framework for direct talks between Washington and Tehran.
Trump, however, offered a different explanation Thursday, saying the purpose of the outreach was to discuss the delivery of medical supplies and humanitarian assistance to Iran.
With Qatar pressing ahead on the diplomatic front and Washington weighing its options after the midterm elections, the gap between the two sides remains substantial. The tanker fires and explosions reported in the Strait of Hormuz have added another dangerous complication to negotiations already overshadowed by the possibility of renewed U.S. military action.

articles.title: Exclusive: US delegation to join Iran talks as war fears grow
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Exclusive: US delegation to join Iran talks as war fears grow
A US delegation is expected to join negotiations with Iranian officials in Doha following a breakthrough in indirect talks between Washington and Tehran, sources close to Qatar- and Pakistan-led mediation efforts told The New Arab on Saturday, as fears grow of renewed war after next week's US midterm elections.
The breakthrough followed more than 12 hours of negotiations in Tehran on Friday involving a Qatari mediation delegation headed by a senior adviser to Qatar's prime minister and foreign minister.
Sources told The New Arab that preliminary understandings had been reached concerning Iran's nuclear programme, navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and financial incentives for Tehran, with China and Russia expected to act as guarantors of any agreement.
However, a source close to the mediation efforts said it remained uncertain whether direct negotiations would take place, although Qatari mediators were seeking face-to-face talks between Washington and Tehran.
An Iranian source confirmed to The New Arab that negotiations were continuing indirectly through mediators, adding that an Iranian deputy foreign minister was in Doha to facilitate discussions with the Qatari delegation.
Axios correspondent Barak Ravid reported that no date had been set for the US delegation's arrival and that no agreement had been reached on resuming direct negotiations.
Iran sets conditions for negotiations
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi described Washington's latest diplomatic outreach as a "positive step" on Saturday, but played down expectations of an imminent meeting with US officials.
"We see no need to meet with the Americans at this stage. Our conditions are clear, and mediators are continuing their consultations regarding them," he told Al Jazeera.
Araghchi said Tehran had reviewed a letter from US Vice President JD Vance during high-level meetings and was considering proposals presented by mediators concerning its nuclear programme.
He also outlined Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, saying Qatar had proposed reducing the implementation period of Tehran's plan to five days before further discussions produced a revised two-day timetable.
"Our conditions include lifting the sanctions imposed following the Islamabad memorandum and reducing US forces in the region," he said.
Tehran was also demanding the restoration of oil export waivers and the release of frozen Iranian assets, including funds held in Qatar.
Araghchi said Iran wanted recognition of shipping routes through the strait previously discussed with Oman, alongside the closure of alternative routes.
Diplomacy races against threat of renewed war
The diplomatic push comes as US President Donald Trump weighs renewed military action against Iran following Tuesday's midterm elections, according to Axios.
The outlet reported that Washington was seeking nuclear concessions before resuming negotiations, while Tehran wanted the US naval blockade lifted, frozen assets released and restrictions on Iranian oil exports eased.
Qatari mediators have reportedly proposed allowing UN inspectors to visit Iranian nuclear facilities damaged during the war in exchange for limited US sanctions relief.
Axios also reported divisions within Trump's administration, with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio sceptical about reaching an agreement, while Vance and presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner favour renewed negotiations.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has meanwhile been lobbying Trump to launch a joint military operation against Iran immediately after the elections, according to the report.
A renewed conflict could trigger Iranian retaliation against Israel and Gulf countries, with Tehran previously threatening strikes on regional oil and gas infrastructure if its own energy facilities are attacked.
Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has ordered the country's armed forces to respond immediately to any renewed US or Israeli attack, without geographical restrictions, according to a statement from his office reported by Axios.
"If the enemies once again launch military or terrorist attacks, it will be the Islamic Republic of Iran's Armed Forces and the Iranian nation that determine when and under what conditions those hostilities will end," Khamenei said.
Araghchi also warned that Iran was prepared for another confrontation.
