"We are prepared for all scenarios," he told Al Jazeera, adding that Iran had upgraded its weapons, addressed military vulnerabilities and tested new systems.
Despite the threats, diplomatic efforts continued in Doha on Saturday following Friday's negotiations in Tehran.
A diplomatic source told Axios that Qatari mediators had remained in regular contact with the White House throughout the Tehran discussions.
"There was positive progress. Talks are still ongoing in an effort to unlock a deal between the US and Iran," the source said.

articles.title: Russia loses about 13 warplanes in a month
articles.body:
- Russia lost about 13 military aircraft from late September through October, including seven Su-34s destroyed by Ukrainian strikes and a Tu-95MS bomber in a crash.
- Two Su-30SMs crashed on Oct. 21, and a Su-57 reportedly burned at Akhtubinsk on Oct. 29, though Russia has not confirmed the Su-57 loss.
Russia’s military aviation has lost about a dozen aircraft in roughly five weeks, including at least seven Su-34 fighter-bombers destroyed on the ground by Ukrainian missiles and drones, a Tu-95MS strategic bomber and two Su-30SM fighters in crashes, and a Su-57 stealth fighter that reportedly burned out during an engine start.
The Ukrainian open-source project Oko Gora counted 11 Russian fighter aircraft and one helicopter lost in October alone, with two more Su-34s partially damaged. Adding the Tu-95MS that crashed on Sept. 29 brings the tally to about 13 airframes since late September. Russia has confirmed only the two crashes during training flights and has not acknowledged losses from Ukrainian strikes.
The heaviest losses fell on the Su-34, the jet Russia uses most to drop glide bombs on Ukrainian cities and front-line positions. On Oct. 4, drones from Ukraine’s SBU security service hit a Su-34 and a Su-35 fighter at Khanskaya air base in Russia’s Republic of Adygea, about 500 km (310 miles) from Ukrainian-held territory, along with an ammunition depot. On the night of Oct. 14-15, Ukrainian Navy Neptune missiles struck Borisoglebsk air base in the Voronezh region, and satellite imagery showed four Su-34s destroyed and two more badly damaged. On Oct. 29, another Neptune strike destroyed two more Su-34s at Marinovka air base in the Volgograd region, with satellite images showing the wreckage at their parking spots.
That puts confirmed Su-34 losses for the month at seven destroyed, or nine counting the two damaged at Borisoglebsk. Ukraine’s military intelligence agency HUR said Russia had about 140 Su-34s of all versions in service as of Oct. 22, and that Russian industry delivered 22 new ones between October 2025 and October 2026, Ukrinform reported. October’s losses alone equal about a third of that annual output.
On Sept. 29, a Tu-95MS bomber crashed on takeoff near Ukrainka air base in the Amur region of Russia’s Far East, killing six of the seven crew members. The Russian Defense Ministry said the aircraft was on a training flight without weapons. Russia no longer builds the Tu-95, which it uses to launch Kh-101 cruise missiles at Ukraine, and it was the first Tu-95MS lost in a crash since 2015.
On Oct. 21, a Su-30SM crashed during a training flight in the Kaliningrad region, and the Defense Ministry said both crew ejected. Russian and Ukrainian outlets reported that a second Su-30SM was lost the same day. Days later, the Russian Knights, the Russian Air Force’s aerobatic display team, announced the deaths of two of its pilots, Col. Oleg Yerofeyev and Lt. Col. Vladimir Kochetov, without saying how they died, and Ukrainian analysts have linked their deaths to the second crash. Russian authorities have not confirmed the connection.
The most unusual loss came on Oct. 29 at Akhtubinsk, the Russian Air Force’s main flight-test center in the Astrakhan region. A Su-57 fifth-generation fighter caught fire during an engine start and burned completely, the Ukrainian open-source channel Absolutely Reliable Source said, publishing satellite images of a burn scar on the airfield. Russia has not confirmed the loss. If verified, it would be the fourth Su-57 lost or damaged this year, after a Ukrainian drone strike in April and a crash near Moscow in July that Russia blamed on a technical malfunction.
The tallies also include helicopters. On Oct. 30, Ukraine’s Third Assault Brigade said it destroyed a Mi-8 transport helicopter in the Luhansk region with two Hornet attack drones after the helicopter landed.
The losses span thousands of kilometers, from Kaliningrad on the Baltic Sea to the Far East. The open-source project Oryx had visually confirmed 205 Russian aircraft destroyed or damaged since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, with the Su-34 the most-lost type at 48.

articles.title: Gulf states scramble to avert another U.S.-Israeli war on Iran they cannot stop
articles.body:
The first of two elections that many believe are the final bell before all out war is resumed against Iran is now complete. Although it seems likely that the efforts to cobble together a governing coalition in Israel, if that is even possible, will take weeks, the American midterms are expected to be the last milestone before the United States and Israel launch a massive attack on Iran.
There is no doubt that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is almost bursting with anticipation of the bloodshed to come. Donald Trump, as always, seems unsure of how to proceed, but seems very uncomfortable with the situation as it stands, while also being unwilling to make the concessions necessary to end this futile, destructive war he started for no good reason.
Iran can do little to deter an American attack, if that is what Trump decides to do. But it can retaliate with devastating consequences, which will be felt by its Gulf Arab neighbors, Israel, and the global economy.
That is why the countries of the newly created Mecca Pact—Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Türkiye—took the dramatic step of meeting Iranian officials in Tehran.
Iran trumpeted the meeting as demonstrating the seriousness with which the Sunni Muslim states take the Islamic Republic, meeting in the Iranian capital rather than in a third country.
Saudi Arabia said the meeting was aimed at mediating between the United States and Iran, but there is no evidence the United States had any part in the planning of this meeting. Indeed, the indications are the opposite; one purpose of the confab was to establish regional dialogue specifically on security matters.
Participants included Pakistan’s Chief of Army Staff Field Marshall Asim Munir, Saudi Minister of Defense Prince Khalid bin Salman, and Turkish Director of National Intelligence Ibrahim Kalin. They met with Iran’s Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei.
The fact that the meeting included leaders of the countries’ respective militaries indicates that the description of the meeting—that it was to deal with regional security—is likely accurate.
And, while little has been made public about the substance of the meeting, it also seems fair to say that there was little progress that could have been made on the major issues—the war with U.S. and the ongoing battles between Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni Ansar Allah.
Little room for negotiations
Regarding Ansar Allah, Saudi Arabia was feeling Iran out to see if they would intervene with the Yemeni fighters whom the Saudis have been unable to defeat.
But Iran doesn’t have much reason to do so. While they could benefit from pulling the Saudis away from the American war effort, the compromises Tehran would have to make are far too great.
Reports out of Israel state that the Saudis offered Ansar Allah $1 billion for a ceasefire. But the Yemeni group will not budge on its understandable demand that Saudi Arabia drop its air blockade of Yemen.
This is not an issue Iran can try to mediate. If they try to get Ansar Allah to compromise on the air blockade, it undermines their argument that the United States must end its sea blockade of Iran.
Iran supports Ansar Allah’s cause, but if they thought they could get concessions from the Saudis on the kingdom’s support for American military efforts, Ansar Allah might find it reasonable to agree to a temporary ceasefire to help their ally.
But they cannot compromise on the air blockade, nor would Iran want them to. As long as Saudi Arabia maintains its efforts to block air traffic in Yemen, they can’t buy their way out of Ansar Allah attacks.
On the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, the Saudis are very worried, as are all the countries of the Gulf and their neighbors. They should be, given that Trump has warned the Gulf states to get ready for a “short, intense military campaign.” Considering that the war started on February 27 was supposed to end in just a few days, or weeks at most, no one is counting on the “short” part. But it is likely to be intense, and that intensity will be felt in Iran and the Gulf Arab states.
The problem for Iran is that its interlocutors can do little to turn Trump’s mind. Even Saudi Arabia, which is in a terrible position right now if the war restarts, has few options outside of registering its reservations with Trump, which it surely has already done.
Türkiye and Pakistan have even less leverage over Trump’s decisions. If he is reckless enough to risk the consequences of restarting the war with Iran, what can they do to stop him?
And those consequences are potentially very dire.
The costs of war
Iran has made it clear that it intends to target data centers, AI hubs, and underwater fiber networks that are the backbone of the internet in addition to oil infrastructure. No one doubts they have the capability of doing so.
The amount of damage that can be inflicted on the world dwarfs anything we’ve seen until now.
That has produced fear among the Gulf states, but it has also produced tension between them and Iran. Gulf states are angry at Iran for targeting them in response to American attacks, but Iran is aggravated because the Gulf states have cooperated with Washington.
This double-edged sword was visible this week when Qatar submitted a proposal for a ceasefire and a path back to negotiations, including reciprocal but revocable steps each side could take, presumably offering each side the assurances they needed to proceed.
But at the same time, Qatar publicly supported the call for Iran to allow international traffic through the Strait of Hormuz unconditionally. That did nothing to help the case for Qatar’s proposal, which Iran eventually dismissed as a collection of random ideas rather than a serious proposal and which Trump ignored.
Vice President JD Vance, who has quietly been opposing the resumption of large-scale fighting, tried reaching out via a letter to Rezaei, but the letter reportedly offered no immediate relief from any of the pressures the U.S. is putting on Iran while demanding that any talks include the nuclear issue, which Iran insists be left to be discussed after its minimal terms are met. In other words, it was just Vance delivering Trump’s unacceptable terms in nicer language.
If that wasn’t enough to make the Vance letter a non-starter, the fact that Vance’s earlier efforts were routinely contradicted by Trump soon after empties the vice president of any credibility, even if Tehran believes he is personally sincere in his desire to avoid another round of full-scale fighting.
This leaves only one hope: that Trump, in his eternally mercurial and indecisive way, will back away from what will be a devastating conflict.
One unknown is how much Trump understands about the danger that an Iranian response presents and how certain it is that a devastating response will be coming.
Trump’s threat of a “short intense” attack would seem to imply that he is being led to believe that the United States can overwhelm Iran with devastating force. Of course, that is exactly what he tried in February, and it failed dismally. Outside of insanity, does he have any reason to think that the same action would produce a different result this time?
It could be that what the U.S. and Israel are planning is a multi-phase attack.
American planners may think the weakness of their initial strike was that they targeted Iranian leadership while devastating large areas of civilian and military infrastructure, believing that this would lead to the collapse of the Iranian government. When that failed, there was no plan B.
It may be that the idea this time is to simply start with doing as much damage to Iranian infrastructure as they can, then pinpoint where the response is coming from and take out those missile and drone launchers.
That is consistent with what Senator Chris Murphy is warning about when he says that what the Trump administration is planning is “insane.”
“It will lead to devastating escalation, and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law. There’s been open reporting as to what we may be planning and the civilian infrastructure that we may be targeting,” Murphy said. “They’ve been asked by the president to develop a plan. Whether they believe it will work or not, I do not know. But the plan that they have developed will lead, in my view, to a prolongment and an escalation of this war that will be devastating for our security interests.”
The result, then, would be one of two things. If the U.S.-Israeli attack is successful, the Gulf states will suffer significant damage, but they can recover and, theoretically, come out with a weakened Iran. But that would mean that what failed in February magically works in November, and there is no evidence to support that expectation.
The other, far more likely scenario is that Iran continues to weather American and Israeli attacks and responds by devastating the Gulf states, further demolishing American positions, and inflicting a far greater degree of damage on Israel than they have in the past.
In that scenario, Gulf oil and civilian infrastructure could be damaged beyond repair. Moreover, given the region’s inherent instability—governed as it is mostly by iron-fisted dictators ruling over states of mixed and often clashing ethnicities drawn up by colonial map-makers—such a scenario could well mean the end of one or more of the Gulf states.
It is that scenario that the Mecca Pact countries are trying to avert.
They are not fools; they knew there was little that Iran could do to change the strategic playing field. Instead, they hoped that sending their top security leaders to Tehran would signal to Washington how concerned they were. They understood that the meeting, by its very existence, would give Iran a diplomatic win and, more importantly, would show that the Mecca Pact is intended to forge a new regional security system that will want to work with Iran, potentially even including it in the group someday.
The Mecca Pact countries, as well as Iran, hope that this message of the region’s strong desire to avert the oncoming catastrophe will convince Trump to back off.
Meanwhile, in Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu is even more incentivized to see the war roar back to life. With the election process in deadlock, he needs to move swiftly, before the opposition can make the case to the public that they are better suited to defeat Iran than Netanyahu.
He needs the war to make it more difficult to replace him, and he will push hard for it. He has already tried to provoke Iran into an act that would have restarted the major fighting before Trump was ready. He will surely try again before too long.

articles.title: Iran warns of unfettered retaliation if attacked as mediators try for peace
articles.body:
Iran warns of unfettered retaliation if attacked as mediators try for peace
Iran’s supreme leader says Tehran’s potential response will not be restricted by geography.
Tehran, Iran – Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has issued a strongly worded message to the Iranian armed forces, as mediators continue to try to prevent a new breakout of war between Iran and the United States.
Senior diplomats from Qatar held extensive talks in Tehran on Friday, with further talks expected to take place on Saturday.
Iranian authorities say they are prepared to respond forcefully amid reports that the US and Israel are preparing for new strikes on Iran.
The office of Iran’s Supreme Leader, Khamenei, who has not been seen or heard from since replacing his assassinated father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in March, said on Saturday that he met with senior military commanders and gave them “important strategic directives”.
Khamenei required “maximum deterrence” through preparedness for “an immediate and effective response, without geographical restriction” if the country is attacked again, according to a statement released by the office.
It comes days after US Vice President JD Vance wrote a letter to Tehran, reportedly addressed to Mohsen Rezaei, the Supreme National Security Council leader who has become a central power in strategic decision-making in Iran despite failing over decades to garner enough votes for public office.
Exact details of the letter are unclear, but Vance is believed to have called for nuclear commitments from Iran, including allowing international inspectors to monitor the country’s nuclear programme and determining the fate of Iran’s highly enriched uranium, which Tehran has said will not be shipped abroad.
Talks
US President Donald Trump earlier rejected reports that he had ordered renewed peace talks, instead claiming without elaborating that the Vance letter was concerned with allowing medical supplies into Iran.
According to Iranian media, Tehran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within several days in exchange for a return to the June memorandum of understanding still remains the baseline for the mediated negotiations.
Tehran’s demands include the lifting of a US maritime blockade on Iranian ports, waivers on oil sanctions, and a truce for regional conflicts, including in Lebanon where Israeli forces continue to occupy the country’s south.
Local media confirmed that Iran received the letter, although they did not say whether any official response has been given through mediators.
An Iranian state-linked Jomhouri-e Eslami (“Islamic Republic”) newspaper published an editorial on Saturday saying that even though the chances of reaching an agreement with the US were slim and fighting could break out after the US midterm elections on November 3, it was still imperative to give a positive response to negotiations and meetings over the coming days.
“We must not allow war to be accepted as the inescapable fate for Iran,” it said.
Iran and the US have kept up their attempts to assert control in the Strait of Hormuz. The IRGC has continued attacking ships and warns of a lingering threat from alleged naval mines. The US military provides guidance and cover for a shuttle system to get oil from Arab states out of the waterway.
Local authorities reported on Saturday afternoon that two fishing boats were bombed by a US drone south of Qeshm island in southern Iran, wounding several fishermen.
Iranian state television claimed late on Friday that at least six tankers, including a very large crude carrier bearing two million barrels of oil, were damaged by explosions after allegedly hitting mines in recent days while transiting “unauthorised” routes in the strait. It also released footage recorded from a small boat close to a larger vessel that was dealing with a fire.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) on Friday reported a new type of attack that occurred a day earlier. It said a tanker was approached by a small boat which attached two explosive devices to the hull above the waterline, resulting in a blast that caused a fire in the engine room and temporarily disabled the vessel northeast of Oman’s Khasab.
The maritime monitor said it recorded 155 inbound and 122 outbound transits through the Strait of Hormuz in the week ending October 28, which was 70 percent lower than pre-war levels.
In a video message on Friday, US Central Command chief Brad Cooper said he flew over the strait and saw dozens of vessels carrying cargo, crude oil and liquid natural gas while being supported by US aircraft and sea drones.
“I didn’t see the IRGC out there at all,” he said. “They patrolled the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters for decades, harassing and threatening and seizing commercial vessels at will. But they were not out there because Iran’s navy is all at the bottom of the sea.”
‘Red lines a thing of the past’
The rhetoric coming from Tehran has only hardened after eight months of war. In line with Khamenei’s Saturday statement, army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia warned the Trump administration against attacking Iran.
“If the US president once more embarks on adventurism in the region through threats and greed of the Zionists, the fire of war will undoubtedly engulf a wider geography,” he said, in reference to Israel.
Other senior officials took aim at Washington’s European allies, who expressed backing for both the US-Israeli offensive on February 28 and last year’s 12-day war.
After German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the costs of war had exceeded 100 billion euros for Europe over the past eight months. Iran’s security chief Rezaei said Europe was “whining” now even though it cheered the war earlier.
“When you cheered on war crimes, did you think the fallout wouldn’t hit you, too? War and terror come at a price. Now it’s your turn to pay,” he wrote on X.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also reminded that Merz had celebrated Israel and the US “doing the dirty work” for Europe during last year’s war.
“100bn Euro is nothing compared to the Earth-shattering blow Iran’s Powerful Armed Forces will deal against those who dare harm our people,” he wrote. “Red lines are a thing of the past”.
US Senator Chris Murphy said earlier this week that he had a meeting with senior officials about what a short and blistering US military campaign would look like if the war resumes.
“Their plan is insane. It will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law,” he said.
Eric Brewer, deputy vice president for the Nuclear Materials Security Program for the US-based Nuclear Threat Initiative, said it is entirely unclear what would be achieved through extensive air strikes against Iran’s infrastructure, considering that Trump earlier this week bemoaned that Iran has focused on rebuilding after earlier attacks.
“There is no military solution for remaining nuclear sites [Pickaxe, Esfahan tunnels], and the program remains generally paused. Striking energy targets is unlikely to cause Iran to capitulate to US negotiating demands,” he wrote on X, adding that Iran will also retaliate across the region if attacked.
“They will aim to make the war not just more painful for the US and its partners, but longer than we would prefer,” Brewer said. “The risks of this operation far exceed any gains.”

articles.title: Araghchi: Iran has no plans for talks with US until its conditions are met
articles.body:
Araghchi: Iran has no plans for talks with US until its conditions are met
TEHRAN — Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said Iran has no plans to hold talks with the United States under the current circumstances, stressing that Tehran will consider direct or indirect negotiations only after Washington accepts its conditions.
In an interview with Al Jazeera, Araghchi discussed the latest diplomatic efforts, a message conveyed by US Vice President JD Vance, proposals put forward by regional mediators, Iran’s conditions regarding the Strait of Hormuz, and the country's military preparedness amid the possibility of renewed confrontation.
He said the message sent by Vance had been carefully reviewed and discussed at high-level meetings in Iran. Araghchi described the initiative to open a channel for dialogue as a positive development, but warned that Washington would be making another mistake if it sought to exploit the initiative to create divisions within Iran.
“The American side’s attempt to open the door to dialogue and broader understanding is a positive step,” he said, adding that if the purpose was to sow discord, it would amount to another mistake by the United States.
Araghchi rejected speculation about an imminent meeting between Iranian and American officials, saying no such meeting was currently planned and that media reports on the matter did not reflect Tehran’s position.
“We see no need to meet with the Americans at present,” he said, emphasizing that Iran’s conditions were clear and that regional mediators were continuing their consultations on the basis of those conditions.
He added that Iran would decide whether any future negotiations should be held directly or indirectly only after the United States agreed to its demands.
Mediators continue diplomatic consultations
Araghchi said regional mediators were continuing their efforts to facilitate an understanding between Tehran and Washington. He noted that Qatar and Pakistan remained involved in the consultations and that an Iranian official had traveled to Qatar to pursue discussions.
“My aide is currently in Qatar to continue consultations,” he said.
The foreign minister also referred to proposals submitted by mediators concerning Iran’s nuclear program, saying Tehran was examining them as part of the second phase of the diplomatic process.
Addressing Iran’s relations with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Araghchi said a considerable distance remained before cooperation with the agency could return to normal.
He stressed that Iran remains a party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) and is committed to fulfilling its obligations under the treaty. Iran’s position on its nuclear commitments, he indicated, should be considered separately from the current difficulties surrounding cooperation with the IAEA.
Iran sets conditions for reopening Strait of Hormuz
Araghchi also outlined Iran’s proposal concerning the Strait of Hormuz, explaining that discussions with Qatari mediators had led to a significant reduction in the proposed implementation period.
He said the Qatari side had initially suggested a five-day period for implementing the proposal, but subsequent consultations had reduced the timeframe to two days.
The Iranian proposal includes several conditions, among them the lifting of sanctions imposed following the Islamabad memorandum, a reduction in the US military presence in the region, the restoration of oil waivers and the release of all Iranian frozen assets, including those held in Qatar.
Araghchi also emphasized that reopening the strategic waterway would require recognition of a new shipping route established by Iran in coordination with Oman, as well as the closure of other routes.
He made clear that the arrangements for maritime traffic through the strait were an essential part of Iran’s proposal and that the reopening process would have to take account of the new route and the understandings reached between Iran and Oman.
The foreign minister further stressed that Tehran sought an end to the war and the cessation of hostilities across all fronts, including Lebanon. He said efforts to end the conflict should not be confined to one front while fighting continued elsewhere in the region.
Iran prepared for all possible scenarios
Turning to the prospect of renewed military confrontation, Araghchi said Iran was not ruling out the possibility of another war and was prepared for all scenarios.
“We do not rule out any possibility regarding the outbreak of war, and we are prepared for all scenarios,” he said.
He explained that Iran had used the period following the previous confrontation to strengthen its military capabilities, upgrade its equipment, address vulnerabilities and test new weapons.
Araghchi stressed that the country’s armed forces were at the highest level of readiness and that Iran was fully prepared to respond to any renewed military action.
 
He also acknowledged the impact of US economic pressure on Iran, but insisted that such pressure would not force the country to surrender or abandon its positions.
“We will continue to stand firm and resist, and we will overcome this difficult phase through our own capabilities,” he said.

articles.title: Zelenskyy thanks US over deal for 500 Patriot missiles but warns delivery could take years
articles.body:
Kyiv has long called for more interceptors to help its forces fend off Russian missile and drone attacks. The rapidly approaching winter is pressing home that need.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has praised the US for its "strong decision" to approve the sale of 500 much-coveted Patriot missiles to Ukraine - but he has warned that delivery could take years.
The US State Department announced on Friday that Washington had green-lit a package of Patriot PAC-3 interceptors worth $2.1 billion as Kyiv continues to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks.
"Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defence package," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on social media in response.
"However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS," he continued. "We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors."
Earlier this week, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had been waiting for almost a month for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on a batch of missiles for both the Patriot and NASAMS systems.
Kyiv has long called for more interceptors to help its forces fend off Russian attacks, and the rapidly approaching winter is pressing home that need. Russia has repeatedly sought to target Ukraine's power grid over wartime winter periods as Moscow has looked to break the country's resolve.
Dwindling stocks of interceptors have already encouraged Russia to ramp up missile attacks in recent months, and there are fears this trend could lead to an especially brutal winter for Ukrainians.
"The United States, our European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses," Zelenskyy said overnight. "Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS, through this production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and our partners would be the right approach."
The Patriot missile platform is one of the world's most advanced air defence systems and can be used to defend against a variety of threats, including incoming aircraft and ballistic missiles.
Ukraine receives the majority of its Patriots through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which facilitates the purchase of military equipment and munitions from the US by allies and partners.
As of June 2026, allies had committed to funding more than $6 billion of defence equipment for Ukraine through the scheme, per NATO.

articles.title: US approves Patriot missiles sale to Ukraine
articles.body:
US approves Patriot missiles sale to Ukraine
The US State Department has green-lit a $2.1 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine.
The announcement follows a report by CNN earlier this month that Kiev had completely exhausted its stockpile of US-made interceptors used to defend against Russian missile and drone strikes at military-related targets.
The State Department said in a statement on Friday that the Ukrainian government had requested that Washington sell it 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles and spare parts for launchers.
Kiev will pay for the interceptors with funds donated by Canada, Germany, and Norway, the State Department said. “No US funds are involved in this sale,” it added.
The principal contractor for the deal will be Lockheed Martin, according to the statement.
“There will be no adverse impact on US defense readiness as a result of this proposed sale,” the department stressed.
The US depleted much of its Patriot missile stockpile during the war with Iran, which was widely reported by American media and confirmed in a Pentagon inspector general’s report last month. A separate Congressional Budget Office assessment said that the Pentagon had consumed between one-half and two-thirds of its inventory of certain missile-defense interceptors since June 2025.
However, US President Donald Trump has downplayed the shortages, claiming that American stockpiles are virtually unlimited.
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky reacted to the State Department announcement in a post on X, saying that he was grateful to Trump and that 500 Patriot missiles was “a substantial number.”
However, he complained that “it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin only in a few years,” while Kiev needs the interceptors “right now.”
Zelensky claimed US and European countries currently have “sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses,” urging Washington to find a solution that would see them supplied to Ukraine immediately.
“The Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day. In just these past two weeks of October, there have already been more than 30 Russian strikes on critical parts of our power grid,” he said.
On Saturday, the Defense Ministry in Moscow said that Russian forces had conducted more drone attacks against logistics and energy infrastructure supporting Ukraine’s war effort. Among other things, a heating and power plant in Kiev and workshops used for production of UAVs and weapons’ parts in Kharkov were hit, according to the ministry.
Moscow says that the strikes are being carried out in response to Ukrainian terrorist attacks on residential areas and civilian infrastructure inside Russia, to which Kiev resorts in order to compensate for setbacks on the front line.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Patriot PAC-3 missile deliveries could take years, while Ukraine needs them this winter
articles.body:
Zelenskyy says Patriot PAC-3 missile deliveries could take years, while Ukraine needs them this winter
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has welcomed the US State Department's decision to approve the sale of interceptors designed to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles for Patriot air defence systems to Ukraine. However, he said deliveries might not begin for several years.
Source: Zelenskyy on social media
Quote: "A strong decision by the US State Department – authorising Ukraine's purchase of Patriot interceptors to counter Russian ballistic missiles. Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defence package. However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS. We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors."
Details: Zelenskyy stressed that, ahead of winter, Russia had launched a large-scale campaign of strikes against the essential services that keep Ukrainian cities and hromadas A hromada is an administrative unit designating a village, several villages, or a town, and their adjacent territories running, targeting electricity, heating and water supply facilities, as well as bridges. He said that in the last two weeks of October alone, Russian forces had conducted more than 30 strikes on key parts of Ukraine's power grid.
The president also said that Kyiv had asked the US to provide a winter support package based on a monthly supply of 100 interceptors for Patriot systems.
Quote: "Five hundred missiles would be enough to protect our skies over the coming months – precisely when it is so important for Ukraine to be in a strong position in negotiations and for Russia NOT to succeed in breaking life in Ukrainian cities and communities."
Details: Zelenskyy noted that the US, European countries and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses.
Quote: "Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026-2027 – and replenishing our partners' arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS, through this production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and our partners, would be the right approach. And it is entirely feasible."
Details: Zelenskyy also thanked US President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, with whom the issue of PAC-3 interceptors had recently been discussed, and the US State Department for approving the deal. He called for decisions that will ensure people's lives are protected at the very moment a threat arises.

articles.title: Why are US, Russia and China racing to put nuclear reactors on the moon?
articles.body:
Why are US, Russia and China racing to put nuclear reactors on the moon?
Lunar reactors could revolutionise moon exploration, providing energy for bases and mining, but risks of contamination remain.
The United States, Russia and China are racing to build nuclear reactors on the moon, as scientists warn about the possible risk of a radioactive mishap.
In January, NASA, the US space agency, announced plans to develop a nuclear reactor on the moon by the end of 2030. Russia, working with China, aims to do the same by 2036 as they strive to advance space exploration.
The reactors will be needed to power mining of frozen water trapped deep in the moon’s craters, which scientists believe could supply drinking water, air, and rocket fuel for future bases. The reactors would also provide power for lunar bases.
Here is what we know.
Which countries want to put nuclear reactors on the moon?
The US said NASA’s Lunar Reactor 1 would produce 20 kilowatts of electricity, creating enough power to run on its own for five years without maintenance.
NASA’s reactor is designed to be compact, weighing under 6,000kg (13,200 lbs) and will fit inside a rocket compartment measuring 3.7 metres (12 feet) long by 5.5 metres (18 ft) wide.
Russia is also building a nuclear reactor, which is expected to produce 10 kilowatts. The reactor, called Selena, will be able to run for a decade without maintenance. It will be ready to power a Chinese-led moon base by about 2036.
The Selena reactor is expected to be even lighter than NASA’s, weighing about 1,100 to 1,300kg (2,400 to 2,800 lbs) for an easier and softer landing on the lunar surface.
This would not be the first time nuclear reactors have been placed in outer space.
The Soviet Union launched more than 30 nuclear fission reactors into Earth’s orbit between the late 1960s and the 1980s to power spy satellites during the Cold War.
The small, 1,000kg (2,200 lbs) reactors powered radar-tracking spy satellites using heat from splitting uranium atoms into 3 to 5 kilowatts of electricity. They are no longer operational, and no other country has sent nuclear reactors into space.
The US has spent $20bn on advanced space nuclear programmes over the past 70 years, but has never successfully launched a nuclear reactor into space since an experiment in 1965.
That experiment was carried out to see if nuclear energy could power a satellite. It worked at first but accidentally shut down after just 43 days because a non-nuclear electrical part of the satellite broke down. It is still floating up in space today.
Previous attempts by the US to develop nuclear projects have stalled due to shifting budget priorities.
How do you put nuclear reactors on the moon?
First, scientists will have to build a reactor on Earth, which will then be transported to the moon using a robotic spacecraft that fires rocket engines for a slow and gentle touchdown.
Both the US and Russia say they would keep their reactors switched off until they reach the moon, to keep radioactive risk at a minimum until the last step.
Once set up on the moon, the reactors would be designed to run without maintenance for years, supplying power to bases engaged in mining on the lunar surface.
Why does the moon need a nuclear reactor?
The US, China and Russia want to build bases near the moon’s south pole, close to the known sources of water ice. The ice sits in the permanently shadowed craters, where sunlight has not reached for millions of years.
As well as powering the moon bases, the reactors would also supply enough power for mining. So far, the US, Russia and China want to mine for frozen water which, once released, could be used to support life on the moon at bases where people could live and conduct research.
Tech billionaire Elon Musk has also said he wants to extract minerals such as aluminium, titanium, and silicon, required for manufacturing satellites.
Solar power for such endeavours would be limited as the sun shines on any one spot on the moon only half the time, so solar panels would go dark for about two weeks every month.
Simon Middleburgh, director of Bangor University’s Nuclear Futures Institute (NFI), told Al Jazeera that solar power is too limited to provide the steady flow of energy a moon base would need, while batteries and diesel are too costly, because everything has to be launched from Earth.
Nuclear energy is the “obvious choice”, Middleburgh said, adding that it must be used “responsibly”.
It is likely that three or four reactors working together would be required to provide sufficient energy for mining lunar ice as well as supporting a moon base, he added.
Why the rush?
It comes down to geopolitics.
In a December 2025 executive order, US President Donald Trump ordered NASA to build a lunar reactor ready to launch by 2030. Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin have revealed similar plans.
In August this year, Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said the US is in a “race to the moon, in a race with China”.
Middleburgh said the 2030 deadline is likely for building the reactor itself, but the harder part will be landing on the moon and safely setting up the system.
“The biggest challenge isn’t really the nuclear technology at all; it is the regulation for launch, the availability of a launch platform itself, and the landing and setting up the system on the lunar surface ready for it to be operated sustainably and safely,” he said.
The race to the moon also comes amid growing military competition beyond Earth. In September, the US announced it had deployed weapons into orbit, which officials said would be used to defend US forces.
While the US did not provide details about these “weapons”, experts say they are likely to be space-based communications jammers, rather than kinetic ones that launch strikes.
The announcement raised concerns about the concept of “space weapons” or the use of space for military purposes, including the potential targeting of satellites that provide GPS, communications and intelligence.
What could go wrong?
Middleburgh told Al Jazeera that an accident during the launch of the reactors would be less frightening than it sounds because uranium alone, before it is used in a reactor, is not very radioactive. However, that changes once the reactor is switched on.
The risk is bigger if a running reactor falls back onto Earth, analysts say.
In 1978, a Soviet satellite carrying a reactor, Kosmos 954, scattered radioactive material across nearly 124,300 square km (48,000sq miles) of northern Canada.
The accident forced an expensive military cleanup of the highly radioactive fragments and microscopic particles.
On the moon, Middleburgh says, any contaminated area would be “extremely localised” if there were to be a similar accident.
Who has sovereignty over the moon?
Legally, no one. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bans countries from “claiming” the moon or any part of it, though they have ownership of the equipment they send there. The treaty does not ban nuclear power in space.
Antonino Salmeri, director of the Lunar Policy Platform, a nonprofit, told Al Jazeera that a reactor can be lawful if it follows the treaty’s principles, including peaceful use and avoiding harmful contamination.
Norbert Schorghofer, a senior scientist at the Planetary Science Institute in Arizona, US, told Al Jazeera all signatories “have the right to mine the lunar surface as long as it is for peaceful purposes”.
Whichever country’s reactor gets to the “best” water ice first could claim a “safety zone”, which would not be a land claim but could operate like one. Salmeri said declaring one creates no territorial rights, but a reactor shuts others out anyway, because nobody wants to enter a radioactive area.
A Lunar Policy Platform report released last month points to another problem: Who is responsible if something goes wrong? The report says existing liability rules have not been designed to regulate the use of long-term hazardous equipment on another celestial body.

articles.title: Iran's Khamenei warns US against attacks, orders military buildup
articles.body:
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has warned that any renewed U.S. or Israeli attack would trigger an immediate and geographically wider Iranian response, ordering the armed forces to expand their target lists, strengthen intelligence capabilities and accelerate weapons production.
In a written message following a meeting with senior military commanders Saturday, Khamenei said Iran would determine the timing and conditions for ending any future conflict if its adversaries resumed military or terrorist attacks.
He ordered the armed forces to prepare an "immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response" to any threat, stressing that maintaining a high level of combat readiness was essential to deterring further aggression.
"Intelligent combat readiness for a powerful confrontation with enemies is a fundamental prerequisite for achieving maximum deterrence," he said.
Khamenei also instructed military commanders to update their target database to bring "all U.S. and Israeli assets, tangible and intangible," within striking range, signaling an effort to broaden Iran's potential targeting capabilities in the event of another confrontation.
The directives included strengthening military intelligence, developing domestic defense capabilities and adapting military doctrine and tactics to emerging threats. He also ordered increased production of ammunition and weapons for reconnaissance, logistical support and combat operations.
The meeting brought together senior military officials, including Maj. Gen. Abdollahi, chief of the Joint Staff of the Armed Forces; Maj. Gen. Hatami, commander of the Iranian army; and Maj. Gen. Vahidi, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
The commanders briefed Khamenei on military readiness along the Persian Gulf coast, in the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman, as well as along the country's northwestern and southeastern borders.
They also reported a significant increase in the production of key ammunition and various weapons systems for reconnaissance, support and combat missions. Khamenei expressed satisfaction with the preparations and asked the commanders to convey his appreciation to military personnel, police officers, Basij forces, Defense Ministry employees and their families.
Beyond military preparations, the supreme leader stressed the importance of strengthening the armed forces' ideological and spiritual foundations while addressing the welfare needs of personnel.
He also described public support as a central element of Iran's deterrence strategy, portraying continued public gatherings across the country as an extension of the national solidarity displayed during the 1980-1988 Iran-Iraq War, which Tehran calls the Sacred Defense.
Khamenei praised the resilience of the so-called Resistance Front, referring to Iran-aligned groups across the region, and highlighted closer coordination among operational fronts as a factor in shaping a new political and security order in West Asia. He expressed hope that such cooperation would encourage greater unity among Muslim nations.
His latest instructions come amid continuing tensions following the U.S. and Israeli military campaign against Iran, which began Feb. 28 and killed then-Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and several senior military commanders.
Iran retaliated with attacks against Israel and U.S. military assets across the Middle East, widening the confrontation and raising concerns about the security of regional shipping and energy supplies.
Although Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum in June following diplomatic efforts, disagreements over regional security arrangements and navigation through the Strait of Hormuz have kept tensions high.
The strategic waterway, through which a significant share of the world's oil shipments passes, has remained a major point of contention, with Iran maintaining pressure on maritime traffic as the U.S. sustains its military presence in the region and reported blockade measures affecting Iranian ports.
Regional diplomatic efforts, including mediation involving Qatar, have yet to produce a lasting resolution.
Iranian army spokesman Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akraminia reinforced Tehran's warnings Saturday, saying a renewed confrontation would spread beyond its previous geographical boundaries if U.S. President Donald Trump launched another military operation against Iran alongside Israel.
"If the U.S. president once again embarks on another military adventure in the region under pressure from and inducement by the Zionists, the flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area," Akraminia wrote on X.
"And the end of the conflict will not be in his (Trump's) hands," he added.
Accusing Washington of repeatedly undermining diplomatic efforts, Akraminia said the Iranian army was continuously strengthening its combat readiness and closely monitoring U.S. military movements across the region.
His remarks came as Tehran and Washington remained at odds over the terms of any lasting settlement, particularly security arrangements and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
Mojtaba Khamenei, who succeeded his father earlier this year, has maintained a relatively low public profile since taking office amid the conflict. His previous warnings have focused on U.S. military bases in the region, the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's conditions for ending hostilities, including demands concerning sanctions, blockades and regional security.

articles.title: Diplomacy or war? Qatar signals Iran breakthrough as US warns Gulf states to prepare for war
articles.body:
Conflicting reports have emerged in the Arab world and the United States over the past 24 hours about what may unfold between Washington and Tehran in the coming week. President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly warned that he intends to bring the war with Iran to an end, one way or another, after the midterm elections, said Friday that he had time. But reports Friday night indicated that the United States had instructed Gulf states to prepare for the possibility of fighting resuming as early as next week. Meanwhile, the Qatari newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed reported Saturday morning that a breakthrough had been reached in talks mediated by Qatar.
The Qatari report, citing unidentified sources, said that "a U.S. delegation will join the talks in Doha to negotiate directly with Iran."
Saudi channels Al Arabiya and Al Hadath reported overnight that they had obtained a draft proposal being discussed by mediators. The purported draft has not been confirmed by any of the parties, including Qatar. According to the reports, it includes a preliminary Iranian commitment regarding the future of its nuclear stockpile; discussions on arrangements to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days; daily talks on confidence-building measures between Iran and the United States; an agreed timetable for implementing commitments by both countries; and a possible role for China as a guarantor of any agreement.
"Any Iranian action regarding its nuclear program will be met by a corresponding U.S. action on sanctions. Clear procedures will be established to address any delays or noncompliance by Iran," the Saudi channels claimed. "Neither Iran nor the United States will be required to make concessions without receiving a corresponding commitment." The reports also referred to "a clear definition of Iran's and the United States' obligations at every stage of the agreement."
The Lebanese newspaper Al-Akhbar, which is affiliated with Hezbollah, reported Saturday, citing "informed sources," that Iran does not oppose mutual commitments regarding the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the lifting of the naval blockade. According to the report, Iran's reservations concern the clause on nuclear concessions, under which Tehran would allow inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) access to its nuclear facilities. In return, Washington would lift some sanctions and release some frozen Iranian assets. Tehran has repeatedly insisted that any negotiations over its nuclear program would take place only after a formal declaration ending the war and concrete steps to that effect.
The reports of negotiations and a possible breakthrough stand in contrast, to varying degrees, with a growing number of reports in the United States suggesting that Washington is preparing to resume the war, potentially as early as next week. U.S. network MS NOW reported Friday that the Trump administration had informed its Gulf allies that they should prepare for a "short and swift" round of fighting that could begin as early as Nov. 4, the day after the midterm elections. Three senior Gulf officials provided the information to the network.
However, Trump said Friday night that talks between the two sides were continuing. "There are talks. They want to talk. They keep talking. We have time, frankly," he told reporters at the White House. He added that the conflict with Iran was "not a typical war" and claimed it was not imposing significant costs on American taxpayers. He also repeated his assertion that the United States had eliminated the nuclear threat posed by Iran. "I spent a lot of money in order to get rid of a nuclear weapon, which we've done," he said.
Earlier Friday, in an interview with Kansas City radio station KCMO, Trump expressed optimism about ending the conflict. "It will end soon," he declared, without explaining how. He emphasized that Washington's central condition for ending the war remained a guarantee that Iran would never possess a nuclear weapon. His remarks came just days before the U.S. midterm elections, scheduled for Tuesday, Nov. 3. Trump has previously made clear that he would not order new strikes against Iran before the elections but has stopped short of promising not to resume military operations afterward.
According to an Associated Press report this week, U.S. officials warned several Middle Eastern countries and Washington's allies of possible renewed strikes against Iran after the elections. The countries were also asked to prepare for potential Iranian retaliation, including attacks on energy facilities and other critical infrastructure across the region. However, two diplomats familiar with the matter stressed that Trump had not yet made a final decision on whether to resume the strikes.

articles.title: War update: 173 clashes on front line over past day, fiercest fighting in Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka sectors
articles.body:
War update: 173 clashes on front line over past day, fiercest fighting in Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka sectors
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine in a Facebook update on the situation as of 8:00 on Saturday, October 31.
Russian forces launched three missile strikes and 75 airstrikes, dropping 255 guided aerial bombs. In addition, Russian invading forces deployed 9,189 kamikaze drones and carried out 3,104 shelling attacks, including 15 using multiple launch rocket systems. Multiple settlements in the Sumy and Chernihiv regions were hit.
Ukraine’s Rocket Forces and Artillery struck a Russian command post and three UAV control points.
In the Northern Slobozhanshchyna and Kursk sectors, Russian forces launched three assaults, carried out four airstrikes using 10 guided aerial bombs, and conducted 169 shelling attacks.
In the Southern Slobozhanshchyna sector, Ukrainian units repelled nine attacks toward Ternova, Mala Vovcha, and Radkivka, as well as near Vovchanski Khutory, Okhrimivka, Sheviakivka, and Putnykove.
In the Lyman sector, Russian forces launched nine attacks toward Druzheliubivka and near Nadiia, Myrne, Zarichne, Lyman, and Dibrova.
In the Sloviansk sector, Russian troops launched two attacks toward Pyskunivka.
Russian forces conducted no assault operations in the Kupiansk and Kramatorsk sectors.
In the Kostiantynivka sector, 20 enemy attacks were recorded. Russian forces launched offensive operations near Kostiantynivka, Sofiivka, and Vilne, as well as toward Mykolaipillia and Zolotyi Kolodiaz.
In the Pokrovsk sector, Russian forces launched 14 attacks, attempting to advance near Novyi Donbas, Bilytske, Krasnopodillia, Dobropillia, and Molodetske, as well as toward Serhiivka.
Russian forces conducted no assault operations in the Oleksandrivka sector.
In the Huliaipole sector, Russian troops attacked nine times, attempting to advance toward Yehorivka, Nove Zaporizhzhia, and Kosivtseve, as well as near Verkhnia Tersa, Hirke, and Bilohiria.
In the Orikhiv sector, Russian forces launched three attacks near Mala Tokmachka.
The enemy conducted no assault operations in the Dnipro River sector.
No signs of Russian offensive groupings being formed were detected in the Volyn and Polissia sectors.
As Ukrinform reported, Russia’s total combat losses in Ukraine from February 24, 2022, to October 31, 2026, have amounted to approximately 1,588,170 personnel.

articles.title: Pentagon facing up to $15 bn in Iran war base damages – WSJ
articles.body:
Pentagon facing up to $15 bn in Iran war base damages – WSJ
Iranian missile and drone strikes have inflicted up to $15 billion in damage on military installations hosting American forces across the Middle East, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday, citing sources and its own satellite imagery analysis. The massive destruction adds to the Pentagon’s mounting war bill, which has already reached nearly $50 billion.
The newspaper’s analysis identified a total of 274 damaged structures across 24 installations with an American military presence. At least 119 buildings at 13 installations were damaged in the opening two weeks alone; the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain was among the hardest hit. Tehran launched a retaliatory wave of strikes following the unprovoked US-Israeli attack which started the conflict on February 28.
An unnamed US official familiar with the matter told the WSJ that the Pentagon estimated damage to bases from Iranian strikes – which became increasingly precise as the conflict escalated – at a minimum of $5 billion. Another WSJ source suggested that the number could potentially be as high as $15 billion.
Many installations are shared with Washington’s regional allies, meaning they could potentially pay for some of the damage, the report says, adding that the Pentagon may elect not to restore some infrastructure at all.
In particular, Washington is reportedly considering pulling back from its installations in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia so that its personnel would be out of reach. Tehran has previously demanded a full-scale US military withdrawal from the region as a prerequisite for sustainable peace.
Iran, meanwhile, has been rapidly restoring missile facilities and recovering buried weapons stockpiles, the report adds, noting that the military build-up comes as US President Donald Trump is considering further strikes despite shortages in American interceptor inventories.
However, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has been dismissive about Tehran’s military potential, saying in August that “They still have some capabilities, but it’s nowhere near what it was at all.”
Meanwhile, Democratic Senator Chris Murphy, a member of the Foreign Relations Committee and the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense, accused the administration of seeking to “mask the true cost of the war” after being denied access to Qatar’s Al Udeid Air Base, where the WSJ identified at least a dozen damaged buildings. The Pentagon said that the ban was due to regional travel restrictions.
According to the Pentagon’s latest estimate provided to Congress, the Iran war has cost $47.1 billion through October 16, excluding base damage. The figure includes roughly $29 billion to replace expended munitions, $11.9 billion in operational expenses, and $6.1 billion in equipment losses.
As for the casualties, the US military now acknowledges 23 deaths linked to Iran war operations, including 11 from enemy fire, and 865 wounded.

articles.title: Russian victories, Spanish tragedy, elections without answers: RT stories that shaped the week
articles.body:
Russian victories, Spanish tragedy, elections without answers: RT stories that shaped the week
Russia’s diplomatic victories
Four years of unprecedented sanctions and an active conflict didn’t deter four dozen African nations from sending delegations to Moscow for the third Russia-Africa Summit this week. Forty-eight out of Africa’s 54 countries were represented at the summit, 21 of them by their heads of state.
More than 140 bilateral and multilateral agreements were signed, including a Russia-Africa Action Plan for 2027-2029, and a joint declaration opposing unilateral sanctions and the unlawful seizure of civilian shipping, pledging deeper counter-terrorism cooperation, and supporting increased African representation on the UN Security Council. RT covered the summit minute-by minute, and broke down Putin’s plan to help bring about the “second awakening” of Africa.
Before he welcomed the African delegations to Moscow, Putin held a rare phone call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb – a figure repeatedly floated as a potential EU envoy to Russia – and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store. Putin later said that Russia welcomes “any steps aimed at restoring full-fledged and comprehensive relations,” and while the call brought the Russia/Ukraine conflict no closer to an end, Russian analyst Sergey Strokan noted that it should serve as a warning to Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky that “metal fatigue is setting in across Europe’s political machinery – and that time is running out for the regime in Kiev.”
With the EU nowhere to be seen, and Stubb and Store incurring the wrath of their fellow European leaders for even daring to speak to Putin, the tone in the US could not be more different. There, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov touched down in Atlanta for a meeting of G20 foreign ministers on Friday. Sanctions on Russian diesel exports have been lifted, trilateral talks between Moscow, Kiev, and Washington are slated for next month, and Putin has been invited to the G20 leaders’ meeting in Florida in December. However, the most tangible result of Russian-American diplomacy came 5,000 miles away from Washington, in the besieged town of Alyoshki.
The Alyoshki breakthrough
Moscow and Kiev agreed to a temporary ceasefire in the frontline town of Alyoshki in Russia’s Kherson Region last Friday, with both sides agreeing to suspend all military operations to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and prepare for civilian evacuations.
The Kremlin confirmed this week that the ceasefire was coordinated by US First Lady Melania Trump, who said she was moved by the plight of Alyoshki’s “elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water.”
Ukraine had accused Russia of preventing civilians from leaving the embattled town, but residents who escaped earlier this month told RT that Alyoshki was besieged by Ukrainian forces, who carried out drone attacks on vehicles carrying food, fuel, and medicine.
As Russian forces got to work clearing mines from the roads surrounding Alyoshki, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that the humanitarian truce, if successful, “could set a precedent” for other areas. The interactions between Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmitry Lubinets, who worked together on the ceasefire, certainly seem to confirm that cooperation is possible.
Three elections, fewer answers
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva narrowly defeated right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday, in the first of three major elections this week. After a first-round loss to Bolsonaro, whose father was jailed last year Brazil’s Lula-aligned Supreme Federal Court, Lula won the runoff election by a margin of 51.79% to 48.21%, securing a fourth term in office.
The drama did not end when the votes were counted. Bolsonaro was ordered by the court to surrender his passports the following day, but he instead fled Brazil to the US, with the help of Argentina’s right-wing government. After landing in Florida, Bolsonaro accused Lula of fraud, declared himself “the leader of Brazil,” and pledged to “lead the opposition” from abroad.
US President Donald Trump is a close ally of Bolsonaro, and it remains unclear whether Washington will turn up the diplomatic pressure on Lula in the wake of the election.
Hours after Lula claimed victory in Brazil, former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic lost his bid to extend his party’s decade in power. Serbia’s Student List defeated Vucic’s SNS party by 53.03% to 38.97%, and despite accusing the students of doing the “dirty work” of “various European countries and the American deep state,” Vucic conceded and congratulated his opponents.
Although the Student List entered politics as an outgrowth of youth-led protests, its base is broader than similar pro-Western movements in the region. Student List representative Jovo Bakic told RT that his party will not sever relations with Russia or impose sanctions on Moscow, while representative Radomir Saicic has promised to negotiate long-term gas contracts with Russia.
However, the Student List has not yet chosen a candidate for prime minister, and Vucic has claimed that the party will walk back these promises in the coming months.
In Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faced voters on Tuesday for the first time since Hamas’ October 7, 2023 attack plunged Israel into a multi-front war. Netnayhu’s opponents – most of whom differ little with the prime minister on matters of war and national security – accused him of corruption, incompetence, and failure to heed forewarnings of October 7. These arguments succeeded in destroying Netanyahu’s right-wing majority, but left neither him nor the opposition bloc in a position to form a government.
Enter the Arabs. Israel’s Arab parties almost doubled their representation in parliament, and are now in a position to play kingmakers – if only Netanyahu’s opponents would work with them. This outcome is highly unlikely, and as RT Middle East correspondent Elizabeth Blade reported, the only certainty is that somebody will be left feeling betrayed.
Spain’s train tragedy
The collision of two high-speed trains near the Spanish city of Toledo on Wednesday was the country’s deadliest railway disaster in more than a decade. At least 69 people were killed and 179 injured when a high-speed Renfe AVE train struck a stationary Iryo train on the Madrid–Seville line.
The crash happened at a time of political crisis in Spain, after weeks of anti-government protests over housing and inflation. While the circumstances are still being investigated, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is already bearing the brunt of public anger, with the right-wing Vox party blaming Sanchez and the left-wing Frente Amplio coalition demanding political accountability.
Fires were set outside the Spanish Transport Ministry in Madrid on Wednesday night, at a protest organized by the far-right Falange and Revuelta groups. “How many more people have to die before we throw these murderers and traitors out of our institutions?” Falange spokesman Federico Campanero said in a speech.
La manifestación frente al ministerio de transportes exigiendo la dimisión de Óscar Puente se calienta. La gente está hasta los cojones. https://t.co/KGcoYNeIjU
— Capitán General de los Tercios (@capTercio) October 28, 2026
Ursula von der Leyen’s Canadian debacle
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen arrived in Montreal on Thursday on what should have been a straightforward mission: secure Canadian energy and resources, expand trade links, and extract money for Ukraine and backing for the EU’s latest push into the Arctic.
Instead, she picked a fight with the EU’s largest member states – France, Germany, and Italy – by insisting that Canada will become an “associate member” of the European Union. Although the term “associate member” is a legal fiction, the French, Germans, and Italians had insisted that she swap it out for “ever closer association.”
Von der Leyen, as her subordinates have repeatedly complained to the press, is not the type to listen.
Star Wars becomes reality
In space, not even Elon Musk’s Starlink network is safe from Israel’s sprawling spy-tech sector. RT has covered the activities of private spies in depth in our ‘Wired for War’ series, and this week it emerged that an Israeli advertising company targeted Starlink users in more than 200 countries with pop-up ads that allowed multiple Israeli spyware companies to plant surveillance software on their devices without their knowledge. The company was the largest purchaser of advertising space targeting Starlink users in more than 100 countries, with the leaderboard – Palestine, Syria, Libya, Yemen, and South Sudan – suggesting that its clients were more interested in picking targets than customers.
Finally, the following video is not taken from an upcoming Star Wars movie, but from Antarctica, where footage of Russia’s revamped Vostok Station went viral this week. Built in 1954, the “sci-fi fortress” received a futuristic makeover in 2024, and now sits on stilts above the snow, 1,500km inland on Antarctica and operating in temperatures as low as -89C.
RT has more fascinating details on the Metal Gear Solid-style complex here, and for more on the coming week’s top stories as they happen – including the pivotal midterm elections in the US – keep an eye on our home page.

articles.title: 'Only we will decide when it ends': Khamenei threatens US and Israel as Iran talks advance
articles.body:
Arab media outlets continued reporting Saturday on alleged progress in negotiations between Iran and the United States aimed at preventing a resumption of hostilities, potentially after the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday. The Qatari newspaper "Al-Araby Al-Jadeed," which earlier reported a breakthrough in the talks, said around midday that an Iranian deputy foreign minister had arrived in Doha, Qatar's capital. The newspaper did not identify which deputy minister had made the trip.
Reuters also reported that Iranian representatives arrived in Doha on Saturday following more than 12 hours of talks in Tehran on Friday. A source familiar with the negotiations told the news agency that Qatari officials were in continuous contact with the Americans but did not confirm reports earlier in the day that a U.S. delegation was also on its way to Qatar.
The reported arrival came as Iran's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, issued a defiant statement following what was described as a meeting with senior military commanders. Once again, Iranian authorities released a written statement attributed to Khamenei without an accompanying photograph. Iran's supreme leader has not been seen publicly since his appointment to the position, or since he was wounded in Israel's opening strike against Iran on Feb. 28, which targeted the residential compound of his father, Ali Khamenei.
According to the Iranian statement, Khamenei warned that if Israel and the United States launched another attack, Iran would determine the timing and conditions for ending the fighting. He added that he had ordered an update to the military's target list to "ensure that all tangible and intangible assets of the American-Zionist enemy" (as stated in the original) would be within the reach of Iranian forces.
Khamenei instructed the senior commanders he reportedly met to maintain combat readiness for a major confrontation and respond to any attack without geographical limitations. He also praised Iran's proxy organizations. According to the report, those who met with Khamenei included Ahmad Vahidi, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps; Ali Abdollahi, Iran's military chief of staff; and Amir Hatami, commander of the Iranian army.
The Qatari report published Saturday morning, citing unidentified sources, claimed that "an American delegation will join the talks in Doha to conduct direct negotiations with the Iranian delegation." It did not specify when that would happen, and, as noted, Reuters quoted a source who cast doubt on that claim. Nevertheless, the report said the move could pave the way for an announcement that negotiations were resuming following an agreement on preliminary measures concerning Iran's nuclear program, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and economic incentives for Iran, with China and Russia serving as guarantors of the agreement.
Saudi television channels Al Arabiya and Al Hadath reported overnight that they had obtained a draft proposal being discussed by mediators. The draft has not been confirmed by either party or by the Qataris. According to the reports, it includes an initial Iranian commitment concerning the future of its nuclear stockpile, discussions on arrangements to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, daily talks on confidence-building measures between Iran and the United States, an agreed timetable for implementing commitments by both countries and a possible role for China as a guarantor of any agreement.
"Every Iranian action concerning its nuclear program will be met with a corresponding U.S. action concerning sanctions. Clear procedures will be established to address any delay or noncompliance by Iran," the Saudi channels reported. "Neither Iran nor the United States will be required to make concessions without receiving a corresponding commitment." The reports also referred to "a clear definition of Iran's and the United States' commitments at every stage of the agreement."
The Lebanese newspaper "Al-Akhbar," which is affiliated with Hezbollah, reported Saturday, citing "knowledgeable sources," that Iran does not oppose reciprocal commitments concerning the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the lifting of the naval blockade. According to the report, Iran's reservations concern the provision dealing with nuclear concessions, under which Tehran would allow inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency to access its nuclear facilities. In return, Washington would reportedly lift some sanctions and release a portion of Iran's frozen assets. Tehran has repeatedly insisted that any negotiations on the nuclear issue would take place only after an official declaration ending the war and the implementation of concrete measures.

articles.title: Roshel has sent nearly 3,000 Senator vehicles to Ukraine
articles.body:
- Canadian manufacturer Roshel says nearly 3,000 Senator armored vehicles have gone to Ukraine, as one of its Senator MRAPs went on display at the Canadian War Museum.
- Canada committed 383 more Senators in February 2026, and Mexico, Moldova and a U.S. federal agency are also buying the vehicle.
Nearly 3,000 Senator armored vehicles built by Canadian manufacturer Roshel have now gone to Ukraine, the company said on social media as it placed one of its first-generation Senator MRAPs on permanent display at the Canadian War Museum in Ottawa.
The figure makes the Senator one of the most numerous Western-supplied armored vehicles in Ukrainian service. Roshel did not give an exact count or say how many of the vehicles were paid for by Canada, by Ukraine itself or by other donor countries.
“Nearly 3,000 Senators have gone to Ukraine, a symbol of Canadian support for those defending their country,” Roshel said.
The company’s tally has climbed steadily since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Roshel said it had delivered 1,400 Senators by the fall of 2024 and more than 2,000 by December 2025, and the Canadian Defence Review put the number at more than 2,700 this week. The Senator is used by Ukraine’s armed forces and its Border Guard Service to carry troops, evacuate wounded and run patrols and reconnaissance.
Canada’s own donations make up only part of the total. Ottawa announced its first package of 200 Senators in January 2023, worth CAD 90 million, and in February 2026 it committed another 383 Senators along with 66 LAV 6 armored vehicles from General Dynamics Land Systems Canada. Other countries have bought Senators for Ukraine through aid packages, and Ukraine has purchased some directly.
The Senator is built on a Ford F-550 heavy commercial truck chassis, a choice that lets Roshel produce it faster and more cheaply than purpose-built armored vehicles. The MRAP version, short for mine-resistant ambush-protected, meets NATO STANAG 4569 protection Levels 2 and 3 and is designed to survive the detonation of up to 8 kg (17.6 pounds) of explosives. Founded in 2016 in Brampton, Ontario, Roshel began building the Senator in 2018, mainly for police and security agencies in North America, before wartime orders from Ukraine expanded its production. Canada’s defense minister said in March that the program supports close to 500 jobs in Brampton and nearby Mississauga.
Roshel also sells the Senator well beyond Ukraine, including to U.S. federal agencies. NASA used a Senator to escort astronauts Bob Behnken and Doug Hurley to the launch pad at Kennedy Space Center for SpaceX’s Crew Dragon Demo-2 mission in May 2020, the first crewed launch from U.S. soil in nearly a decade. In November 2025, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement awarded Roshel a sole-source contract worth about $7.3 million for 20 Senator emergency response vehicles, CBC News reported, citing procurement records that said only Roshel could deliver within 30 days. ICE said the vehicles qualify under Buy American rules because they are produced in the United States; Roshel opened a plant in Michigan in 2024. The deal drew criticism from some Canadian politicians and advocacy groups over ICE’s immigration enforcement. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives is also buying a Senator for its special response team.
Elsewhere, Mexico selected the Senator MRAP earlier this year after trials with its armed forces and national guard, and Moldova’s military is due to receive more than 100 Senators funded by the European Union by May 2027. The company has also supplied vehicles to Haiti, Brazil, South Korea, Costa Rica and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

articles.title: Japan’s FM urges Russia to release journalist detained on Sakhalin
