articles.title: House Democrats Demand Trump Preserve Grok AI Chats After TIME Report
articles.body:
The top Democrats on the House Judiciary and Oversight Committees are demanding that President Donald Trump preserve his conversations with artificial intelligence chatbots as part of an inquiry into whether Elon Musk’s AI system Grok has influenced official White House policy. The demand offers a preview of the intense scrutiny Trump would face in the final years of his presidency if Democrats reclaim the House in next week’s midterm elections.
In a letter to Trump, unveiled Oct. 30, Representatives Jamie Raskin of Maryland and Robert Garcia of California call on the President to preserve “any prompts” submitted to AI chatbots, including Musk’s Grok, OpenAI’s ChatGPT, and Anthropic’s Claude, while “carrying out your constitutional, statutory, or other official or ceremonial duties,” along with the responses the chatbots generated. They also request a briefing on the matter by 5 p.m. on Nov. 11. Raskin and Garcia would be in line to chair the Judiciary and Oversight Committees, respectively, if Democrats win the House.
The request stems from a TIME report earlier this month detailing a previously undisclosed December 2025 meeting between Trump and Musk in the Oval Office. According to an official who was present, Trump spent hours asking Grok questions about his presidency and legacy.
At the time, Trump was ordering missile strikes on Venezuelan boats he alleged were smuggling drugs into the United States. He asked Grok how Venezuelans would react if the U.S. captured President Nicolás Maduro. The chatbot responded that Maduro was a repressive and deeply unpopular dictator whose downfall many Venezuelans would likely celebrate, the official said. The following month, Trump ordered a military operation to seize Maduro, and celebrations erupted in the streets of Venezuela. Trump came away convinced that Grok was ingenious, according to officials familiar with his thinking.
The lawmakers cited TIME’s reporting that Trump sought Grok’s “advice on carrying out some of your presidential duties,” including asking it to opine on how Venezuelans would respond to Maduro’s capture. Just “weeks later,” they noted, Trump “ordered the U.S. military, without congressional authorization, to attack Venezuela and capture President Maduro.”
They called the episode “deeply troubling,” arguing that Trump “consulted Grok—but not Congress—on your military deployment to Venezuela, circumventing Congress’s constitutional power to declare war and introducing instead into American foreign policy decision making a technology that is highly manipulable and demonstrably error-prone.” The White House’s use of AI chatbots, they warned, “exposes the United States to acute national security risks” and leaves the country vulnerable to “malign influence from unknown and unaccountable third parties.”
A Trump Administration official says that the White House “preserves all required records in accordance with the law” but declined to answer specific questions stemming from the letter. A spokesperson for Musk did not respond to requests for comment.
The preservation demand rests on the Presidential Records Act, enacted in the wake of the Watergate scandal, which makes presidential records the property of the public and requires that they be filed separately from personal materials. In 2014, lawmakers passed amendments that extended the law to include electronic records. The principle of preservation, the statute said, applied to the content of the information rather than the medium that holds it, a standard that on its face would seem to reach chatbot exchanges tied to official duties.
But the statute itself does not mention AI, and the most direct federal guidance, from the National Archives, covers agencies under the separate Federal Records Act. That language treats prompts and outputs as likely records only if they are captured and saved in an agency system, a caveat critics say limits its reach for commercial chatbots. In April, the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel declared the Act unconstitutional, although the White House has told a court its staff are still preserving materials related to their work. A federal judge ordered the administration in May to preserve presidential records for now.
The dispute comes as Democrats are preparing for the possibility of reclaiming congressional investigative powers after two years in the minority. A Democratic-controlled House could use committee hearings, document requests, and subpoenas to examine how Trump and his advisers have conducted official business, including the extent to which emerging technologies have entered the administration’s decision-making process.
Whether the White House complies with the Democrats’ demand, ignores it, or fights it could offer an early glimpse of the confrontations that await Trump in the final years of his presidency.

articles.title: Strikes blamed on Houthis target Yemen presidential palace
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Strikes blamed on Houthis target Yemen presidential palace
Yemen's Houthis targeted the presidential palace in Aden on Friday with two missiles, a police official told AFP, hours after Saudi forces said they had intercepted an attack by the group on the Gulf kingdom.
Aden, the seat of Yemen's Saudi-backed and internationally recognised government, has been targeted repeatedly since Yemen's dormant civil war reignited in July.
Two eyewitnesses told AFP they saw ambulances entering the palace in Aden, a large compound made up of several buildings including facilities used by government and Saudi-led coalition forces, after the incident.
Shortly before, residents and an AFP journalist said they heard two blasts in the city.
The Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa to the north, most recently struck the perimeter of Aden's airport on Wednesday after saying they had targeted a naval base and a military camp last week.
The coalition, which is fighting the Iran-backed Houthis, said on Friday it had intercepted and destroyed a drone near the Saudi capital of Riyadh, as well as a missile fired towards the country's southern region.
In two posts on X, coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said forces had destroyed the drone in Riyadh province as well as "a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the southern region".
Earlier on Friday, the coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone in the Mecca region, with the group denying it targeted Islam's holiest city.
"A drone launched by the terrorist Houthi militia has been intercepted and destroyed in the Mecca region," Malki wrote in a post on X.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree called the Saudi statement "a massive and egregious fabrication".
Hours later, Malki reported another drone interception, this time over the Medina region, home to Islam's second holiest city.
Yemen's war began in 2014, with Saudi Arabia entering the conflict in support of the government the following year.
A ceasefire in 2022 brought relative peace until this summer, when the conflict reignited.
More than a decade of warfare has created a humanitarian catastrophe in one of the world's poorest countries, which the UN estimates is home to 42 million people.

articles.title: Advanced new naval anti-air missiles to arrive later this year
articles.body:
Deliveries of new Aster Block 1 missiles will begin later this year, and considerable progress has been made over the past twelve months in upgrading the existing stock to the same standard, though the number converted so far is being withheld on security grounds, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what progress has been made on upgrading all Royal Navy Aster missiles to Block 1 standard through Sea Viper Evolution Capability 1.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence, said: “The upgrading of missiles to Aster Block 1 standard is being undertaken through the Aster Mid-Life Refresh programme. The exact number of missiles upgraded to date cannot be disclosed owing to security concerns, however considerable progress has been made over the last 12 months. Additional deliveries of new Aster Block 1 missiles will commence later this year.”
Aster is the missile family behind Sea Viper, the air defence system carried by the six Type 45 destroyers, and the Block 1 standard brings an improved capability against ballistic missiles as well as aircraft and cruise missiles. Sea Viper Evolution is the wider upgrade programme announced after HMS Diamond and HMS Richmond spent months intercepting Houthi drones and missiles in the Red Sea, where the Royal Navy fired Aster in anger for the first time.
Stock depth has been the question hanging over that capability since those engagements, because a destroyer carries forty-eight cells and an intercept uses one missile or two. Replacing what was expended and raising the standard of what remains are the two halves of the same problem, and the department has consistently declined to put numbers on either.
Aster is produced by MBDA, with final assembly in France and significant British content including the Sampson radar and the command and control system from BAE Systems. The Defence Investment Plan commits £6 billion to munitions this Parliament, including £1.5 billion for an always on production pipeline.

articles.title: Iran war damage to US bases may cost billions in reconstruction: Report
articles.body:
The financial toll of the Iran war is mounting beyond battlefield losses, with hundreds of buildings at US military installations across the Middle East damaged in Iranian strikes, potentially adding billions of dollars to the cost of the conflict, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday.
An analysis of satellite imagery found that 274 structures at 24 installations with a US military presence sustained damage during the war’s first six months.
Among the hardest-hit sites was Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, where an Iranian strike on July 17 killed three American service members and damaged at least 19 buildings, including facilities where troops sleep.
READ: Iran warns war could spread ‘much wider’ if US launches ‘another military adventure’
The Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that rebuilding the damaged structures alone would cost more than $4 billion, excluding the replacement of equipment and systems inside the buildings.
Meanwhile, the Pentagon has put the damage to US military bases at a minimum of $5 billion, with estimates potentially reaching $15 billion, according to US officials cited by the Journal.
These expenses come on top of the estimated $47.1 billion cost of the war as of Oct. 16, the report said.
Beyond the financial burden, the destruction has raised concerns over the safety of military personnel, with more than 20 US servicemembers killed and over 400 wounded since the conflict began Feb. 28.

articles.title: Iran envoys meet Qatar mediators as threat looms of US strikes after midterm elections
articles.body:
Iran envoys meet Qatar mediators as threat looms of US strikes after midterm elections
- Iranian and Qatari mediators met in Doha as diplomats tried to stop fresh fighting after the US midterm elections. Talks are linked to regular contacts with Washington.
- Marco Rubio said Trump has not decided on new strikes against Iran and prefers diplomacy, though he still has military options. Trump has delayed action while Republicans seek to keep Congress.
- Iran warned of a strong reply to any attack. Khamenei ordered the armed forces to be ready, while Qatar, Iran and the US discussed seven-day trust-building plans, but both sides have rejected key proposals.
AI generated
DUBAI/ATLANTA - Iranian negotiators held talks in Doha with Qatari mediators on Oct 31 to discuss paths out of war in the Gulf, a source told Reuters, as diplomats try to avert a new outbreak of fighting after the US midterm elections this week.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Oct 31 that President Donald Trump has not decided whether to launch new strikes against Iran, but would prefer to resolve the conflict diplomatically.
Trump has held off on strikes on Iran, in recent weeks, ahead of elections at which his Republicans are trying to retain control of Congress.
The Oct 31 talks in the Qatari capital followed more than 12 hours of discussions on Oct 30 between Iranian and Qatari envoys in Tehran, said the source, who was briefed on the negotiations and spoke on condition of anonymity.
The source said the talks were being coordinated in regular contacts with Washington.
Countries in the region have been anticipating that Trump could restart attacks once the voting is over. Iran has repeatedly said it would respond to any new attacks by striking at US and Israeli targets in neighbouring countries.
Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei issued a statement on Oct 31 ordering the armed forces to be prepared to respond to any attacks.
The Iranian military later announced it was taking steps to improve its readiness.
“Any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response,” Khamenei, who has not appeared in public since replacing his father, slain at the war’s outset, said on Oct 31 in the statement posted on his official Telegram account.
Khamenei said that senior commanders had reported high readiness along the Gulf coast, in and around the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman, and on Iran’s northwestern and southeastern borders.
Rubio, hosting foreign ministers of the Group of 20 major economies in Atlanta, declined to set a timeframe for the talks in Qatar, but said direct and indirect contacts with Iran were under way.
“There are multiple talks. Talks have actually never stopped,” he said.
Trump would “prefer to solve it diplomatically. But I think what the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it,” Rubio said.
Diplomacy continues, despite gaps
Trump, who launched the war alongside Israel in February, has repeatedly hinted at plans to restart strikes on Iran. Last week, he called on Israelis ahead of their own election to keep his wartime ally Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in power, so the two leaders can “finish the job”.
But Washington has also lately taken steps to indicate it is open to diplomacy. Earlier this week, Vice-President J.D. Vance, who led the US delegation at previous rounds of talks with Iran, wrote a letter to a hardline senior Iranian security official, which the New York Times and Wall Street Journal described as an initiative to see if it was possible to restart talks.
Trump has played the letter down, saying he approved it only to discuss the possibility of letting more medical supplies into Iran: “I said if you want to do that, that’s OK. Basically, it’s getting supplies in to help people that are not well.”
In the latest Qatari-mediated discussions, the Qataris brought a proposal to Tehran a week ago for a seven-day plan, under which the US and Iran would take daily steps to build trust ahead of broader peace talks, the source briefed on the negotiations said. A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Oct 30 that this proposal was not deemed satisfactory by Tehran.
Iran has been proposing its own seven-day plan since September, so far rejected by Trump. That calls for Washington to lift a blockade of Iranian ports, unfreeze assets and approve an Iranian-backed route through the Strait of Hormuz, after which the contested strait would be reopened.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said in remarks reported by Al Jazeera on Oct 31 that Iran was studying Vance’s letter. He said the Iranian plan was the only proposal on the table to reopen the strait. REUTERS

articles.title: Japan urges Russia to release detained journalist, calls for lasting peace in Ukraine
articles.body:
Saadet Gökce
31 October 2026•Update: 31 October 2026
Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi urged Russia on Friday to release a detained Japanese journalist and take steps toward a just and lasting peace in Ukraine during talks with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov.
The ministers met on the sidelines of the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Atlanta, the US, where they discussed bilateral issues and the war in Ukraine, according to a Japanese Foreign Ministry statement.
Motegi made a "demarche and an argument regarding various current issues between Japan and Russia," the ministry said.
He "strongly demanded" the immediate release of a Japanese national detained in Russia's Sakhalin Oblast on suspicion of espionage, according to the statement.
Russia's Federal Security Service earlier this month accused a correspondent for the Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk bureau of Japanese newspaper Hokkaido Shimbun of collecting and storing information on Russia's defense capabilities for Japanese intelligence.
The agency said the information could be used against Russia's security and opened a criminal case against the journalist, while Moscow's Lefortovo District Court ordered the journalist's arrest pending an investigation.
 
- Japan calls for lasting peace in Ukraine
Motegi also raised the war in Ukraine during the meeting, reiterating Tokyo's position on the conflict.
He "once again strongly called on Russia to take positive actions toward achieving a just and lasting peace in Ukraine," the Japanese Foreign Ministry said.
They agreed to remain in contact "even amid the severe situation in Japan-Russia relations," according to the statement.
Relations between Japan and Russia have deteriorated sharply since Moscow launched its war against Ukraine in February 2022, prompting Tokyo to impose sanctions on Russia.

articles.title: U.S. approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
articles.body:
U.S. approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, but Zelenskyy warns deliveries would take years
The State Department approved on Friday the sale of 500 Patriot missile defense systems to Ukraine at a cost $2.1 billion.
In a statement released Friday, the State Department said the purchase will be paid for by Ukraine with donations from Canada and European allies such as Germany and Norway, and that no U.S. funds are involved in the sale.
"This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe," the department said. It also added the principal contractor in this agreement is Lockheed Martin and that there would be "no adverse impact" on U.S. defense readiness.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy lauded the decision, and thanked President Trump, but warned that it may take years for the munitions to be delivered to Ukraine.
"We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger," Zelenskyy appealed on Friday evening.
In a post on X, the Ukrainian president said there had been more than 30 Russian strikes on his country's energy infrastructure in the past two weeks, targeting "the systems that sustain life in our cities and communities."
He appealed to the United States and European allies to provide Ukraine with the Patriot systems currently in their own stockpiles and replenish their arsenals with these 500 missiles, purchased by Ukraine, in the coming years.
"We are asking for decisions that can guarantee the protection of lives not the day after tomorrow or sometime later, but at the very moment the threat is there," Zelenskyy added.
Ukraine has long warned of dwindling supplies of Patriots, which it uses to intercept strikes from Russia, and has previously accused the U.S. of slowing down deliveries of the critical missiles.
The development comes amid ongoing tensions between Ukraine's president and Mr. Trump, who faced criticism for waiving new sanctions on Russia just days before they were expected to take effect.

articles.title: Flu Vaccine Now Required for Many Airmen, Guardians, and DAF Civilians
articles.body:
Airmen and Guardians in the Active and Reserve component, as well as civilian employees, in “mission critical and high-risk populations” are now required to receive influenza vaccinations annually to “preserve force readiness,” according to a recent Department of the Air Force memo.
The Oct. 20 memo, signed by Assistant Secretary of the Air Force for Manpower and Reserve Affairs Richard Anderson, directs personnel in six population categories get vaccinated for seasonal influenza:
- Recruits, training populations, and congregate living
- Rapid deployment forces and “no-fail” missions
- Deployed forces
- Health care personnel
- Civilian personnel in child development and youth services programs
- Air Mobility Command aircrew supporting U.S. Transportation Command taskings, enroute care personnel, and executive airlift personnel
The guidance memo, which was posted on the unofficial Air Force amn/nco/snco Facebook page, comes more than three months after a flu outbreak at Air Force Basic Military Training left one recruit dead and infected more than 280 others at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, Texas.
An Air Force spokesperson confirmed the memo is authentic. Air Force Times was first to report on the memo.
Airmen and Guardians in deploying units should align their vaccinations with pre-deployment timelines. All other personnel included in the policy must be vaccinated no later than Dec. 15 annually, the memo states.
“For service members in the designated populations, vaccinations are a requirement; failure to comply may result in administrative or disciplinary action under the Uniform Code of Military Justice,” the memo states. The memo, however, adds that “commanders should consider using the lowest level of discipline … when evaluating options to address noncompliance, taking into consideration the circumstances of the noncompliance and previous disciplinary record of the Airman or Guardian.”
For civilian employees in the identified populations, flu vaccinations are considered a condition of employment, the memo states. Supervisors “should not take adverse action indecently” but should but address noncompliance through the “Civilian Personnel Section/Human Resources in coordination with Labor and Employee Relations,” the memo states.
The new guidance partially rolls back Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s April announcement that he was rescinding the mandate for Active-Duty troops and trainees to receive the annual flu vaccine. Hegseth said in a video posted on social media at the time that “the notion that a flu vaccine must be mandatory for every service member, everywhere, in every circumstance at all times is just overly broad and not rational.”
The Pentagon approved the Department of the Air Force exception-to-policy request on June 11, the memo states.
“The DAF requested an exemption to the voluntary policy to protect mission-critical and high-risk populations,” according to the memo. “The mandatory vaccination for these select groups [is] deemed essential to preserve force readiness, prevent illness, minimize lost duty days, and ensure the successful execution of DAF missions.”
Airmen, Guardians, and civilian personnel in the designated populations can submit requests for religious accommodations and medical exemptions for the flu vaccine mandate, the memo states, adding that personnel who have their request denied will have an opportunity to comply with the vaccination requirements.
The memo includes detailed descriptions of each population and in some cases offers examples where some personnel will be exempt from the requirement. For example, personnel that fall under the “recruits, training populations and congregate living” category are “excluded” if they are assigned to single-occupancy dorm rooms—such as permanent party—unless they are “assigned to or routinely perform duties in hig- risk environment.”
Another example in this population applies to Air University and other non-technical training organizations whose “primary mission is professional military education, doctrine, graduate education, and other non-technical instruction will not be included solely because they conduct resident education.”
It’s unclear what percentage of Department of the Air Force military and civilian personnel are now required to take the flu vaccine. After the flu outbreak at Lackland, only around 40 percent of Air Force trainees took the flu shot after Hegseth made it optional, The Associated Press reported. That’s a little lower than the 46.5 percent of American adults who got the shot this past flu season, according to the CDC.
Vaccine “hesitancy” has surged in recent years. A mandate in 2021 that all service members receive COVID-19 vaccinations fueled an intense political debate. Around 8,000 service members ultimately were separated for refusing the Pentagon’s mandate, and the Pentagon has taken steps to allow some members to return.

articles.title: Rubio defends decision to invite Russia to G20 meetings
articles.body:
Rubio defends decision to invite Russia to G20 meetings
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has sought to defend Washington's invitation for Russia to participate in G20 meetings, emphasising the need to continue interaction with the Russian side.
Source: Rubio at a press conference in Atlanta following the G20 ministerial meeting, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Journalists asked Rubio to comment on criticism from his European counterparts regarding Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov's participation in this week's G20 ministerial meeting and the invitation of Russian leader Vladimir Putin to the summit in Miami.
Rubio responded that he considers Russia's participation in G20 discussions important, particularly due to US diplomatic efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
Quote: "In order to end the war in Ukraine peacefully, you're going to have to have a negotiated settlement... How can you have a negotiated settlement between Russia and Ukraine if you don't have the ability to talk to both Russia and Ukraine? How can you talk to both Russia and Ukraine unless you interact with them?"
Details: Rubio said Lavrov's participation in the G20 ministerial meeting is another "opportunity to continue to interact with the Russian system".
Quote: "As I've said to you earlier in my conversations, the president does not view meeting with someone or talking to someone as legitimising everything they do or everything they stand for."
Details: According to Rubio, everyone wants to see a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, but it is impossible to make one without dialogue with Moscow.
Quote: "If we can play a role in mediating an end to that conflict, the United States is prepared to play that role. And to play that role, we have to have the ability to communicate with both sides. We talk to the Ukrainians plenty. We talk to them as much, if not more, than we talk to the Russian side."
Details: Rubio specifically stressed that Russia, like the US, is a nuclear power, and therefore Washington and Moscow must maintain dialogue to avoid dangerous escalation.

- The US has invited Putin to the December G20 summit in Miami, where he may hold a meeting with Trump.

articles.title: Delivery of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine will not begin before 2030

Zelenskyy said 500 missiles would help protect Ukrainian skies in the coming months and strengthen Ukraine's position in negotiations. He stressed that the US and other partners had sufficient PAC-3 stocks to supply Ukraine during the winter of 2026-2027 and could replenish their arsenals in subsequent years through already contracted and funded production.
US Senator Richard Blumenthal also said it was a "disappointing catch to the announcement about interceptors going to Ukraine – delivery in a few years".
"Facing a hideously harsh winter & searing hardship from Russian bombs, Ukraine urgently needs air defence. America's green light to immediate aid would be lifesaving," he stressed.

- On 30 October, the US Department of State approved a potential agreement to sell Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) missiles for Patriot air defence systems to the Ukrainian government.

articles.title: Iran warns war could spread ‘much wider’ if US launches ‘another military adventure’
articles.body:
Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akraminia, spokesperson for the Iranian army, said Saturday that renewed war would “engulf a much wider area” if US President Donald Trump “resorts to another adventure in the region” alongside Israel, Anadolu reports.
“If the US president once again embarks on another military adventure in the region under pressure from and inducement by the Zionists, the flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area,” Akraminia wrote on US social media company X.

articles.title: Iran holds US and Israel responsible for disruption of maritime Security
articles.body:
Iran holds US and Israel responsible for disruption of maritime Security
TEHRAN – Iran’s Ambassador and Chargé d’Affaires to the United Nations in New York, Gholamhossein Darzi, has said the United States and the Israeli regime bear direct responsibility for any disruption or obstruction of maritime navigation in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, warning that their continued acts of aggression and maritime restrictions threaten the security of the entire region.
 
Addressing a meeting of the UN Security Council on October 29, Darzi rejected attempts to hold Iran responsible for disruptions to maritime traffic, arguing that the current situation was the direct consequence of military aggression against Iran and measures targeting its civilian and maritime infrastructure.
 
He stressed that Iran had consistently upheld maritime security and freedom of navigation in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz for decades, fulfilling its responsibilities as a coastal state.
However, he said, some participants in the Security Council meeting had once again overlooked the root causes of the current situation.
“The responsibility for any disruption, obstruction, or other interference with maritime navigation in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz lies directly with the aggressors and those who facilitate or assist their acts of aggression against Iran,” Darzi said.
He added that such actions had endangered maritime safety and freedom of navigation throughout the region, describing attempts to shift responsibility onto Iran as unfounded and lacking credibility.
Iran cites attacks on vessels and maritime infrastructure
Darzi said the Strait of Hormuz and the maritime trade route passing through it had remained open until February 28, 2026, when the United States and Israel launched a 'war of aggression against Iran.'
He accused the two sides of continuing their unlawful actions, including deliberate attacks on Iran’s civilian and maritime infrastructure, ports and vessels.
To illustrate the consequences of these actions, the Iranian diplomat cited several incidents involving Iranian naval and commercial vessels.
He said a US submarine sank the Iranian frigate Dena in international waters in the Indian Ocean on March 4, killing more than 100 Iranian sailors.
On April 19, US military forces attacked the Iranian commercial vessel Toska, he added.
Darzi also referred to a statement by the US Central Command (CENTCOM), saying that by May 23, US forces had redirected 100 commercial vessels and disabled four others in enforcing the maritime blockade.
He further said that on July 23, US forces attacked two Iranian search-and-rescue vessels, Naji-15 and Naji-16, in Iranian territorial waters while they were engaged in humanitarian operations.
Tehran denounces US maritime blockade as violation of international law
The Iranian envoy said Washington had imposed a blockade on maritime traffic entering and leaving Iranian ports since April 12, describing the measure and its military enforcement as a flagrant violation of Iran’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
He argued that the blockade constituted a serious breach of Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, which prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state.
Darzi also warned that restrictions on maritime traffic threatened civilians’ access to food, medicine, fuel and other essential supplies, potentially depriving the population of necessities indispensable to their survival.
He characterized the consequences of the blockade as a form of collective punishment and called for accountability for the resulting harm to civilians.
Iran invokes its right to self-defence
Rejecting accusations against Tehran, Darzi described Iran’s measures as defensive and lawful, emphasizing the country's right, as a coastal state, to protect its sovereignty, territorial integrity, population and vital national interests.
“As a coastal State, Iran has the legitimate right, under international law, to take all necessary and appropriate measures to protect its sovereign rights, its territorial integrity, its people, and its vital national interests against the US ongoing threat or aggression,” he said.
The diplomat called for full accountability for 'serious violations of international law' and the damage and suffering inflicted on civilians.
He urged the UN Security Council not to remain silent in the face of these developments and called on the body to explicitly demand that Washington immediately end its unlawful actions.
Darzi concluded by reaffirming that Iran would pursue all available legal avenues to ensure that those responsible were held accountable.
A call for the Security Council to address the root causes
At the beginning of his remarks, Darzi also addressed the role of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, in maritime security.
 
He acknowledged that such technologies could create opportunities to improve maritime safety while simultaneously introducing new vulnerabilities. However, he stressed that the Security
Council should focus on genuine threats within the framework of its mandate under the UN Charter and respect the responsibilities of competent international bodies.
His remarks underscored Tehran’s position that maritime security in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz cannot be separated from the broader security environment and the consequences of military action against Iran.
Iran maintains that ensuring safe and uninterrupted navigation in the strategic waterway requires an end to military aggression, respect for the sovereignty of coastal states and compliance with international law.

articles.title: “European countries need to learn”: Ukrainian defense-tech CEO warns Europe against costly defense mistakes
articles.body:
Europe is raising its defense budgets, but a Ukrainian defense-tech executive warns against spending the money on expensive systems that prove too ineffective to stop cheap drones at a sustainable cost. That is the case Taras Bublyk, CEO of the Ukrainian electronic-warfare firm UNWAVE, made in an interview with Ukrinform.
He argued that economics decides these fights: firing a costly missile at a cheap drone every time is a defense no budget can sustain for long. Bublyk said Europe should learn from the lessons of the Russo-Ukrainian war.
Why a missile for every drone is a losing trade
Bublyk said the core problem is the price gap between a threat and the tools used to stop it. Spend an expensive missile each time to down a relatively cheap drone, and the defense cannot be sustained.
“The cost of countering must be proportionate to the cost of the threat. The countermeasures must be affordable, produced in sufficient quantity, and work as a single system,” Bublyk explained.
His answer is a layered defense that combines detection, electronic warfare, interceptor drones, physical barriers, and conventional air defense, so that where jamming or a cheaper interceptor will do, no one burns a costly missile.
Advanced weapons are not the same as being ready to use them
For Europe, that means investing not only in the technology but also in integrating it and scaling up production because owning advanced weapons does not, by itself, mean a country can use them well.
Rising European defense budgets are a good sign, he adds, but risk flowing to systems built without the lessons of the current war.
“There is a risk of investing in expensive systems that may prove insufficiently effective. European countries need to learn to integrate drones, electronic warfare and other technologies into specific combat tasks, taking Ukraine’s experience into account,” he said.
Ukraine has previously offered to teach what it has learned under constant drone attacks and jamming.
The rules that could cost Europe precious minutes
Much of Europe’s critical infrastructure is still underprepared for modern drone threats, Bublyk continued, and even sites with some protection often run systems designed without real combat experience, while Ukraine, which has that experience, is ready to help.
“European countries should use Ukraine’s experience of protecting critical infrastructure and move now from planning to building and deploying the relevant systems,” he said.
He also pointed to a regulatory gap: many European states restrict the use of electronic warfare, including in certain frequency bands, with no clear rules for switching such systems on in a real emergency.
Responsible agencies, he argued, need clear authority and fast-response mechanisms, so no one loses precious time seeking permissions once a threat has already been detected.

Finnish President Alexander Stubb has denied media reports that Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin lectured him and the Norwegian prime minister on history during a phone call.

Finland is not acting as a mediator in the negotiations but fully supports Ukraine, Stubb stressed. He said Finland stands 100% with Ukraine and that Putin had been told this directly.
Stubb acknowledged that the phone call with Putin had drawn criticism from some leaders but said he is not concerned about a rift between the Nordic countries.
The Finnish president stressed that all the Nordic countries share exactly the same goal in this matter, namely supporting Ukraine and facilitating the peace talks, so he is not worried in this regard.

articles.title: Turkey nominates former FM in race for next UN chief
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkey throws its former foreign minister's name into the race for next UN chief
Turkey has officially nominated a former foreign minister and yearslong ambassador to the United Nations for the next UN secretary-general, state-run media reported Saturday.
The next UN chief will succeed António Guterres, who has led the world body for almost 10 years. The organization is under pressure to reform as it finds itself sidelined in wars in Iran, Ukraine and Gaza while also facing a financial crisis that has forced major cuts to humanitarian and development programs.
Feridun Sinirlioglu, a 70-year-old former Turkish foreign minister and UN diplomat, had floated his candidacy on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly’s high-level meeting in New York last month.
Sinirlioglu was Turkey's top diplomat for a few months in 2015, an interim period between elections, and its UN ambassador between 2016 and 2023.
He currently serves as the secretary-general of the Vienna-based Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe. His current three-year mandate is scheduled to end in December 2027, but the top UN job would have a Jan. 1 start date.
Ahmet Yildiz, Turkey’s current representative to the UN, told the Anadolu news agency that Sinirlioglu's name was officially submitted with backing from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Erdogan has been vocal in calling for reform of the UN Security Council, especially criticizing the dominance of its five permanent members. Sinirlioglu is likely to reflect the president’s agenda.
The next UN secretary-general will be decided by the 15-nation UN Security Council, especially its five veto-wielding members — the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France. The 193-member General Assembly must give final approval.
Sinirlioglu will likely face obstacles from several corners, including Turkey's neighbor Greece, which is one of the 10 elected members of the Security Council. Pushback also would be expected from Israel, a close ally of the United States.
Seven other candidates are vying to replace Guterres as he finishes his second five-year term. Under an informal regional rotation of the UN’s top job, a candidate from the Latin American and Caribbean region could be selected.

articles.title: Europe has blown its chance to mediate Ukraine conflict – Lavrov
articles.body:
Europe has blown its chance to mediate Ukraine conflict – Lavrov
European countries have repeatedly failed to uphold agreements intended to resolve the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, undermining their credibility as potential peace guarantors, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said.
Moscow previously stated that European officials would not take part in the upcoming US-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi.
Speaking at a press conference on the sidelines of a G20 meeting in Atlanta, Georgia on Friday, Lavrov said “the Europeans want to insert themselves into the negotiation process.”
“What matters is not what the Europeans want, but what added value they can actually bring to the table.”
Lavrov accused European governments of failing to uphold agreements intended to resolve the crisis, beginning with the February 2014 deal between then-Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovich and opposition leaders. France, Germany, and Poland helped broker the agreement, which was intended to end months of protests and deadly clashes in Kiev.
Yanukovich was ousted shortly afterward, an event Moscow maintains prompted Crimea to secede from Ukraine and join Russia, while also triggering a revolt in the largely Russian-speaking Donbass.
According to Lavrov, France, and Germany also failed to ensure that Ukraine implemented political reforms and granted special status to Donbass under the 2014-2015 Minsk agreements which they helped broker.
Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel and former French President Francois Hollande acknowledged in separate interviews in December 2022 that the agreements gave Ukraine time to strengthen its military. Moscow cited their remarks as evidence that Western governments never intended to implement the accords in good faith.
Lavrov also cited the December 2019 summit in Paris, where the leaders of Russia, Ukraine, France, and Germany reaffirmed their commitment to implementing the Minsk agreements. The diplomatic process ultimately failed to produce a lasting settlement.
“Over the past 12 years, they have had more than enough opportunities. Through their actions, they have demonstrated that their track record cannot be ignored the next time they seek to act as ‘guarantors,’” Lavrov stated.
His remarks followed a rare telephone conversation on Tuesday between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store. The 90-minute call, which focused on the Ukraine conflict and upcoming peace negotiations, drew criticism from several European leaders. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the initiative had not been coordinated with other European countries; Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said he was not informed in advance.
Putin welcomed the contact, describing it as a step toward establishing “some kind of constructive dialogue.”
Lavrov attended the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta at the invitation of the US, despite objections from some European governments to Russia’s participation. US President Donald Trump has also invited Putin to the G20 leaders’ summit scheduled for December in Miami.
European opposition to Russia’s participation was evident on Friday when the traditional G20 group photograph was canceled after several European diplomats objected to posing alongside Lavrov.

articles.title: Iran's military chief says armed forces compile new list of "enemy" targets, assets

articles.title: Erdoğan, Zelensky meet on war and Black Sea security

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan condemned attacks on shipping in the Black Sea on Oct. 31 and pledged continued talks to restore safe navigation after meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Istanbul.

He said the recent escalation had spread the conflict into the Black Sea and that Türkiye would continue discussions with the parties to restore maritime safety.
Zelensky said he and Erdoğan had agreed to work on the Black Sea grain corridor to ensure it operated effectively.
They also discussed the possibility of holding meetings in Türkiye, he said.
The Ukrainian leader said Black Sea issues had occupied a substantial part of their discussions, adding that Russia’s aggression since 2014 had worsened the situation.
Erdoğan welcomed increased efforts to end the war through diplomacy, particularly those involving U.S. President Donald Trump, and said Türkiye was ready to help pave the way for peace.
“A just peace has no losers,” he said.
Erdoğan offered condolences to Zelensky and the Ukrainian people for those killed in the war.
He also said Turkish companies that had remained in Ukraine could make an important contribution to the country’s reconstruction.
Erdoğan welcomed Zelensky with an official ceremony at his Dolmabahçe office before the leaders held one-on-one and delegation-level talks.
Ahead of the meeting, Zelensky said on X that his team was working to strengthen Ukraine’s security, deepen its partnership with Türkiye and pursue diplomatic opportunities.
He highlighted shipping in the Black Sea as an important issue.
The Ukrainian leader made the working visit at Erdoğan’s invitation.
Communications Director Burhanettin Duran had said the agenda would also cover broader regional and international developments.
Defense Minister Yaşar Güler and National Intelligence Organization chief İbrahim Kalın were among the officials attending the talks.

articles.title: Iranian delegation arrives in Doha to discuss nuclear proposals
articles.body:
DOHA, October 31. /TASS/. An Iranian delegation has arrived in Qatar to discuss mediators’ proposals on the Islamic Republic’s nuclear program, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera.
"The mediators have put forward proposals on the nuclear issue, which we are now examining as part of the second phase," the Qatari broadcaster quoted him as saying. "An Iranian delegation has traveled to Doha, and my aide is in Qatar to continue consultations," Araghchi added.
Saudi broadcaster Al Arabiya earlier reported, citing sources, that Iranian authorities had formed special committees to discuss the nuclear proposals.

articles.title: Iranian army chief of staff: Passive defense key to national resilience against emerging threats
articles.body:
Iranian army chief of staff: Passive defense key to national resilience against emerging threats
TEHRAN –Army Chief of Staff and Deputy Coordinator Rear Admiral Habibollah Sayyari has stressed the strategic importance of passive defense in safeguarding the country’s critical infrastructure, maintaining essential services and strengthening national resilience against emerging and increasingly complex threats.
In a message issued on October 30 to mark Iran’s National Passive Defense Day, Sayyari emphasized that sustainable security depends on anticipating threats, reducing vulnerabilities, and ensuring preparedness before crises emerge.
Sayyari said modern warfare and recent conflicts had shown that threats were no longer limited to conventional military confrontations but were increasingly extending to critical infrastructure, supply chains, communications networks, and the economic and social foundations of countries.
Under such circumstances, he said, passive defense should be regarded not merely as a defensive requirement but as a strategic component of national security, essential to preserving national capabilities, ensuring the continuity of vital services and strengthening the country's ability to withstand multidimensional threats.
Sayyari emphasized that, in contemporary security calculations, national power is measured not only by conventional military capabilities but also by a country's capacity to prevent threats, maintain essential functions, and remain resilient during crises.
He described passive defense as a proactive approach to national security, highlighting the importance of identifying potential vulnerabilities and taking preventive measures before adversaries can exploit them.
Referring to the growing complexity of security challenges, the senior military commander said the experience of recent wars had underscored the need for comprehensive preparedness across different sectors of society.
He noted that disruptions to infrastructure, supply networks and communications systems could have consequences extending well beyond the immediate security sphere, affecting economic activity, public services and social stability.
This, he indicated, makes coordination among relevant institutions and the strengthening of the country's passive defense capabilities essential to maintaining national stability and ensuring the uninterrupted operation of vital systems.

articles.title: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine for $2.1 bln — State Department
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, October 31. /TASS/. The United States has approved the sale to Ukraine of 500 PAC-3 missiles for the American-made Patriot PAC-3 air defense system, along with related equipment, for $2.1 billion.
The US Department of State and the Defense Security Cooperation Agency (DSCA), a Pentagon agency responsible for foreign military sales under government-to-government agreements, announced the decision.
The statement noted that the purchase would be "funded entirely by partners and allies." The delivery will include "PAC-3 MSE classified and unclassified spare parts; and other related elements of logistics and program support."
According to Washington, "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe."
US authorities said Ukraine would pay for the missiles with funds provided by Canada, Germany and Norway, as well as through an EU loan. "No US funds are involved in this sale," the statement said. The US authorities also said that "the proposed sale will improve Ukraine's capability to meet current and future threats by improving its integrated air and missile defense capability."
The missiles will be supplied to Ukraine by Lockheed Martin, one of the Pentagon’s key contractors. The statement said that implementing the deal "will not require the assignment of any additional US Government or contractor representatives to Ukraine," and that there will be no adverse impact on US defense readiness as a result of this proposed sale.
The US administration has already notified Congress of the decision. Lawmakers now have 30 days to review the agreement and potentially block it.

articles.title: SNP defence policy attacked by UK Defence Secretary
articles.body:
The Defence Secretary has called the Scottish National Party’s support for unilateral nuclear disarmament a white flag policy and said the party must explain how it would square that with membership of a nuclear alliance, according to remarks made to reporters in Glasgow.
Wes Streeting was asked about the First Minister’s repeated claim that the government in Westminster is leaving Scotland short of defence.
He said: “We’ve got HMS Prince of Wales currently out on a major exercise now, so I think it’s very visible proof that what the First Minister said is both irresponsible and unfounded. I don’t think the SNP should be playing party politics with national defence and security. We’d much rather work with us.
“In terms of the risk of leaving the UK with insufficient defence, one of the biggest risks facing that security is the SNP’s position on unilateral nuclear disarmament. It is by far and away the most important deterrent that we have, and it’s not just the UK’s deterrent, it’s NATO’s deterrent. So any time the SNP says that a separate Scotland can be a NATO member, they have to first explain how their white flag policy on unilateral nuclear disarmament would work under a nuclear alliance.”
The question has followed the party since 2012, when its conference voted by a narrow margin to drop opposition to NATO membership while keeping opposition to nuclear weapons, a position that would require an independent Scotland to join an alliance whose strategic concept rests on nuclear deterrence while removing the British deterrent from Faslane and Coulport.
Every member of NATO except France takes part in the alliance’s Nuclear Planning Group, and the three countries that joined most recently signed up to a strategic concept describing nuclear weapons as the supreme guarantee of allied security. New members are admitted by unanimous agreement of the existing ones.

Residents leave Russian-occupied Oleshky in evacuation operation
Residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky have left for Russia's Anapa city with a Ukrainian delegation, senior official David Arakhamia said Friday. They are expected to fly to Belarus before returning to Ukraine by bus, during a rare ceasefire brokered by the United States.

Some residents of Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in southern Ukraine ravaged by food and medicine shortages, left on Friday during a rare ceasefire brokered by the United States.
Captured by Russia in 2022 and caught in the so-called "kill zone" near the front line, residents had faced supply shortages for months, with some being forced to hunt and eat pigeons, former residents said.

The fragile ceasefire – announced by US First Lady Melania Trump last week to pave the way for evacuations and deliveries of humanitarian aid – is due to end on Sunday evening.
Ukrainian and Russian officials visited the town together on Friday, delivering aid and marshalling those who wanted to leave.
After hours there, both sides said they had left with convoys of people – some heading to Russia, others on a journey back to Kyiv-controlled parts of Ukraine via Russia and Belarus.
"The Ukrainian delegation, along with the evacuated residents of Oleshky, set off for Anapa," Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia said on Friday, referring to a southern Russian city on the Black Sea coast.
"From there, they will fly to Belarus and then travel home by bus," Arakhamia said.
Moscow said the operation had been completed "without any incidents".
"The humanitarian mission in Oleshky is concluding," Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova said in a video post on Telegram.
"Everything went smoothly," she said, saying 25 buses and nine ambulances had been deployed for the evacuations.
Neither side disclosed how many people left.
The pre-war population of Oleshky has dropped from 24,000 to about 2,000.
Read moreAid mission set to enter Ukraine's Oleshky as localised ceasefire holds for third day
Now in its fourth day, the truce is the longest pause in fighting anywhere on the front line since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets posted videos of himself talking to locals – several of whom thanked him – crying and wiping tears.
Groups of residents were seen waiting outside their buildings with bags of belongings ready to leave.
"We've been through so much here in these five years," one woman said in images broadcast on Ukrainian TV.
"If we had our health, maybe we'd stay there a bit longer, but that's it. We just want to be with our children," said another elderly woman preparing to evacuate.

Refinery attacks
Previous partial ceasefires between Ukraine and Russia – for instance, around Orthodox Easter – have been marred by accusations of violations.
The recent respite has also given residents in the major southern Ukrainian city of Kherson relief from daily drone attacks.
The truce has held despite unabated attacks elsewhere in Ukraine.

On Thursday, a drone strike on a train station in the city of Dnipro in central Ukraine killed at least 15 people, while an attack on the northern city of Chernigiv killed two teenage girls.
Russia meanwhile said Ukraine had resumed its attacks on Russian oil refineries after a brief pause following criticism of the strike campaign by US President Donald Trump.
Videos on Russian Telegram channels showed smoke billowing from an oil refinery in Russia's Samara region, following a drone attack overnight.
Trump had been pressuring Kyiv for weeks to stop such attacks, blaming them for the rising cost of diesel.
The latest salvos come as Russia and Ukraine are due to meet next month with US envoys in the United Arab Emirates in a bid to revive talks towards ending Europe's worst conflict since World War II.
No date has yet been set for the Abu Dhabi meeting, but Zelensky said Ukraine wanted it to take place before the potential three-way talks between the Russian, US and Chinese leaders.

articles.title: Israeli army launches fresh airstrikes, machine-gun fire in southern Lebanon
articles.body:
The Israeli army carried out fresh airstrikes, an explosion and machine-gun fire across southern Lebanon early Saturday, Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency reported.
The attacks came despite a US-brokered framework agreement signed by Lebanon and Israel in June and renewed diplomatic efforts to address security disputes between the two sides.
Israeli strikes and military operations targeted several locations across southern Lebanon, including the districts of Nabatieh, Bint Jbeil and Marjayoun, according to the news agency.
In Nabatieh district, Israeli warplanes struck an area between the towns of Nabatieh al-Fawqa and Kfar Tebnit.
Another Israeli airstrike targeted the outskirts of Baraachit in Bint Jbeil district, the agency said.
In Marjayoun district, Israeli forces carried out an explosion in the town of Tallousa, while a drone flew at low altitude over nearby towns, according to the report.
It said that Israeli forces also opened machine-gun fire from the direction of Khiam toward agricultural land in Ibl al-Saqi.
Israeli warplanes separately struck an area between the towns of Adshit al-Qusayr and Taybeh.
READ: Israel blows up homes, shells towns in southern Lebanon
In Tyre district, Israeli drones flew at low altitude over the city of Tyre and surrounding towns, reaching both banks of the Litani River in the Qasmiyeh area.
According to an Anadolu correspondent, Israeli drones have continued flying over Beirut’s southern suburbs since the morning.
Attacks follow US-sponsored talks in Florida
The latest Israeli attacks followed US-sponsored military and technical talks between Lebanon and Israel in Tampa, Florida, on Oct. 20-21.
The meetings ended without an announced breakthrough or a joint statement.
Reports indicated that the sides agreed to continue negotiations, although disagreements remained over Israel’s withdrawal from Lebanon and the disarmament of Hezbollah.
The June framework agreement provides for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from occupied Lebanese territories in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army and the disarmament of armed groups.
Despite the agreement, Israel has continued military operations in Lebanon.
Since March 2, the attacks have killed at least 4,386 people, wounded 12,407 others and displaced more than 1 million people, according to the Lebanese Health Ministry.

articles.title: Poland facing coup d’état – top court
articles.body:
Polish president storms into besieged court amid constitutional crisis (VIDEOS): As it happened
The longstanding power struggle between Poland’s right-wing, Euroskeptic president and its pro-EU government over control of the country’s top court escalated dramatically on Friday night as riot police surrounded the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw.
The latest stand-off was triggered by Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, a judge backed by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government, who ordered the suspension of the Constitutional Tribunal’s president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and vice president, Bartlomiej Sochanski.
Police were deployed as an announcement of their suspensions appeared on the court’s website, from which their profiles were reportedly removed.
Shortly afterward, the tribunal’s official X account claimed that its website had been subjected to an “unlawful takeover” and insisted that both officials remained in their posts. “All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d’état,” the account stated.
Piotrowska meanwhile assumed the role of acting head of the tribunal, citing her seniority as a judge. However, the court’s existing leadership disputes her authority and maintains that Swieczkowski remains its president.
Protesters gathered outside the court building, denouncing what they described as an attack on the tribunal by Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

“We are deeply saddened that Donald Tusk is taking us back several decades, reducing us to a second-class country,” Patryk Jaki, a PiS member of the European Parliament, said.
“Why is Donald Tusk doing this? His main reason is the Constitutional Tribunal’s ruling that Polish law takes precedence over European law,” he added, according to Onet.
According to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), Swieczkowski entered the tribunal’s grounds after his supporters cut through a gate lock with a circular saw. He subsequently left the grounds and called for calm.
Police, meanwhile, established an additional security cordon outside the courthouse. Three people were detained for climbing over the fence.

— Pan_komentator (@PanP23929) October 30, 2026
Police said they had deployed officers following requests from the prosecutor general and Korwin-Piotrowska. The requests cited possible threats to judges and staff and the risk of public disorder. Police denied entering the court building, saying their operations were confined to its grounds and surrounding public areas.
Tusk defended what he described as efforts to restore the rule of law following the previous government led by the conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party. “After years of lawlessness under PiS, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way,” he wrote on X.
President Karol Nawrocki cut short a planned trip to Senegal and turned his plane around to return to Poland amid the escalating crisis.
After landing in Warsaw, Nawrocki held an emergency meeting with Zbigniew Kapinski, the head of Poland’s Supreme Court. After midnight, Nawrocki arrived at the tribunal, physically pushing his way past judges standing in the doorway, according to video footage on social media. There, he confronted both Piotrowska and her fellow coalition-backed appointees Krystian Markiewicz and Maciej Berek, telling them “you are not judges of the Constitutional Tribunal.”
In a statement later, he said that “the constitutional order of the Republic of Poland was violated and a constitutional body of state was forcibly seized” while urging parliamentary consultations to restore order.
Shortly after midnight on Saturday, US Ambassador Tom Rose issued a cautiously worded statement, noting that “both sides offer sharply different accounts of what happened and why.” He urged all parties to avoid violence, warning that “the last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals into something far worse.”
What caused Poland’s constitutional crisis?
The bitter dispute dates back to 2015, when the outgoing parliament, controlled by the pro-EU Civic Platform (PO), appointed five Constitutional Tribunal judges shortly before losing power. While the court subsequently ruled that only two out of five appointments were invalid, the EU-skeptic PiS government replaced all five.
During its eight years in power, PiS introduced sweeping judicial reforms and brought public broadcasters under tighter government control, triggering mass protests. The EU has also repeatedly criticized the party’s judicial reforms, accusing it of undermining judicial independence, while PiS defended them as necessary to strengthen Poland’s sovereignty and accused Brussels of interfering in the country’s internal affairs.
After returning to power in 2023, Tusk pledged to undo the PiS-era reforms, and his coalition refused to recognize the tribunal’s legitimacy. The standoff intensified after PiS-backed Karol Nawrocki won the presidency in 2025 and refused to administer the oath to five of eight tribunal judges elected by parliament in 2026.
How do Poland’s rival camps differ?
Law and Justice (PiS), led by Jaroslaw Kaczynski and which supports Nawrocki, is a nationalist-conservative party emphasizing Catholic traditions, family values, and national sovereignty. Its electoral strongholds have characteristically included rural areas and smaller towns. The party is skeptical of deeper EU integration and frequently clashes with Brussels, although it has not formally sought to withdraw from the bloc.
Civic Coalition, led by Tusk, is a centrist, liberal-conservative and strongly pro-EU alliance, with its electoral base concentrated in major cities. Tusk previously served as president of the European Council from 2014 to 2019. His current government also includes centrist and left-wing allies.
Both camps are strongly pro-NATO and pro-US, but Nawrocki is closely aligned with US President Donald Trump, who endorsed his presidential bid; Tusk is connected to the EU bureaucracy.
Both sides have supported Ukraine in its fight against Russia, but Nawrocki has taken a tougher line on Ukrainian refugees’ welfare benefits and demanded that Kiev stop honoring nationalist paramilitaries who collaborated with Nazi Germany during the early stages of the invasion of the Soviet Union and took part in massacres of Polish civilians in what is now western Ukraine.
On the contrary, Tusk has adopted a more conciliatory approach, emphasizing the importance of continued support for Ukraine in its conflict with Russia.
This concludes our live coverage of the events in Warsaw.
